lessons.title: The actor's instrument
lessons.summary: Your body, voice and imagination are the instrument, and all three can be trained.
objectives: You will do a full physical and vocal warm-up
You will stand in neutral
You will say what acting actually is
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Warm up: shake out, stretch, breathe, hum, articulate
- Find neutral: balanced, open, no habit, no slouch
- Watch a classmate walk and name one thing their body says

## Understand it

A musician has an instrument they can hold. An actor's instrument is **themselves**: the **body**, the **voice** and the **imagination**. Like any instrument, all three can be trained — and like any instrument, they need warming up before they play.

**The body.** Audiences read bodies before words. How someone stands, walks, holds their head and uses their hands tells us who they are and how they feel. Most of us carry **habits** — slouching, crossed arms, fiddling — that we do not notice. An actor first learns **neutral**: standing balanced, weight even on both feet, spine long, shoulders released, arms loose, breathing low and easy. From neutral, any character can be built; from your habits, every character looks like you.

**The voice** needs breath support from the belly, an open throat and clear **articulation** (lips, tongue and teeth shaping each sound).

**The imagination** makes the situation real enough to respond to truthfully: *where am I, who am I with, what do I want, what just happened?*

A warm-up prepares all three:

![A five-step warm-up in order: shake out and stretch, breathe low and slow, hum then open to vowels, articulate with tongue-twisters, then a moment of focused stillness.](media:arts/warm-up.svg)

1. **Shake out** and stretch to release tension.
2. **Breathe** low and slow — hand on belly, feel it move.
3. **Hum** to wake the voice gently, then open to vowels.
4. **Articulate** with tongue-twisters, slowly then faster.
5. **Focus** — a moment of stillness and attention.

Observing people is part of the training too: in a market or a bus park, every person is a lesson in what bodies say.

## Key words

- **Neutral:** a balanced, relaxed, habit-free stance that characters are built from
- **Articulation:** shaping sounds clearly with lips, tongue and teeth
- **Warm-up:** exercises that prepare body and voice to perform
- **Habit:** an unconscious way you move or speak

## Read and watch

- [GCSE Drama](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/subjects/zbckjxs) — BBC Bitesize
- [RSC education resources](https://www.rsc.org.uk/education) — Royal Shakespeare Company

## Practise at home

1. Five-minute warm-up daily
1. Watch people in a market and copy one person's walk

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** Work on one short moment rather than the whole scene. A truthful ten seconds is worth more than a whole page rushed.
- **If you already can:** Play the same moment three different ways and say which is strongest and why.

## Assessed this week

**Practical (6 marks) —** Lead yourself through a warm-up and hold neutral for 30 seconds.

Your instructor watches you do it and marks against this week's three objectives, two marks each. The written check below is worth one mark: this is a practical subject and it is marked like one.

lessons.title: Status
lessons.summary: High and low status, how it shows in the body, and how it changes a scene.
objectives: You will play high and low status physically
You will switch status mid-scene
You will spot status in a real conversation
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Walk the room as high status, then low — change only the body
- Two-person scene: one high, one low, then swap halfway
- Watch a real conversation and name who has status

## Understand it

**Status** is how much power or importance a person shows in a moment — not their job title, but how they behave. The idea comes from the improvisation teacher Keith Johnstone, and it is one of the most useful tools an actor has, because every interaction involves a little status play.

**High status** often shows as: stillness, taking up space, a steady gaze, slow and complete movements, speaking without hurrying or filling silences, touching your own face or head rarely.

**Low status** often shows as: small or fidgety movements, making yourself smaller, looking away, quick or hesitant speech, "um"s and apologies, touching your face.

![High status: stillness, taking up space, a steady gaze, slow complete movements, no rush to fill silence. Low status: fidgeting, looking away, hesitant speech, touching the face.](media:arts/status-signals.svg)

Key insights:

- **Status is played, not owned.** A king can play low status with his mother; a gateman can play high status with a nervous visitor.
- **Status changes during a scene** — and those changes are often the most interesting moments. Watch who gains and loses power, and how.
- **Status is relative.** Raising yourself or lowering the other person both shift the balance.
- Great scenes often have **status reversals**: the confident one is suddenly caught out.

Exercise: play the same short line ("Can I help you?") high status, then low, and watch how completely the meaning changes. Then watch a Nollywood scene with the sound off and say who has the power, moment by moment.

## Key words

- **Status:** the power or importance a character shows in a moment
- **Status shift:** a change in who holds power during a scene
- **Physicality:** how a character uses their body

## Read and watch

- [GCSE Drama](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/subjects/zbckjxs) — BBC Bitesize
- [RSC education resources](https://www.rsc.org.uk/education) — Royal Shakespeare Company

## Practise at home

1. Play three everyday actions at high status, then low
1. Notice status in one real conversation this week

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** Work on one short moment rather than the whole scene. A truthful ten seconds is worth more than a whole page rushed.
- **If you already can:** Play the same moment three different ways and say which is strongest and why.

## Assessed this week

Your instructor watches you do it and marks against this week's three objectives, two marks each. The written check below is worth one mark: this is a practical subject and it is marked like one.

lessons.title: Objective, obstacle, tactic
lessons.summary: What your character wants, what is in the way, and what they try — the engine of every scene.
objectives: You will name your character's objective as a verb
You will name the obstacle
You will play three different tactics
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Write your objective: "I want to..." — an action, not a feeling
- Name what stops you getting it
- Play the same line three ways: charm, threaten, beg

## Understand it

Every scene is driven by three questions, an idea that comes from the great Russian teacher **Konstantin Stanislavski** and is used by actors worldwide:

1. **Objective — what does my character want?** Make it active and aimed at the other person: "to make her forgive me", "to get him to lend me the money". Not "to be sad" — you cannot play a feeling, only an action.
2. **Obstacle — what is in the way?** The other character's refusal, fear, a secret, time running out. Without an obstacle there is no drama: if he lends the money at once, the scene is over.
3. **Tactic — what do I try?** Characters use many tactics: charm, plead, flatter, threaten, joke, guilt-trip, bargain, ignore. When one fails, they **change tactic**. Those changes keep a scene alive.

![A character wants an objective (to get the loan); an obstacle (he refuses) stands in the way; the character tries tactics — charm, plead, guilt-trip — changing each time one fails.](media:arts/objective-obstacle.svg)

Write tactics as **verbs you do to the other person**: *to charm, to reassure, to accuse, to tease, to beg*. Then play each line with its verb.

Why this works: audiences are gripped by people **trying to get something** against resistance. A scene where both actors just say their lines "with feeling" is dull; a scene where one is fighting to get something and the other is resisting is alive — even if the words are ordinary.

Keep a note of your objective, obstacle and tactics for this week's scene; you will return to it in week 7.

## Key words

- **Objective:** what a character wants from the other person
- **Obstacle:** what stops them getting it
- **Tactic:** an action used to try to get it
- **Action verb:** a verb you do to someone, like 'to charm'

## Read and watch

- [GCSE Drama: Stanislavski](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/subjects/zbckjxs) — BBC Bitesize
- [RSC education resources](https://www.rsc.org.uk/education) — Royal Shakespeare Company

## Practise at home

1. Write objective and obstacle for a scene you know
1. Play one line five different ways

## Make it fit you

- **If you already can:** Play the same moment three different ways and say which is strongest and why.

lessons.title: Improvisation: yes, and
lessons.summary: Accepting what your partner offers and building on it, which is also how scripted scenes work.
objectives: You will accept an offer instead of blocking it
You will add something new each turn
You will say what blocking does to a scene
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Play "yes, and" in pairs — accept and add, never deny
- Play a scene where someone blocks, and feel it die
- Build a three-minute improvised scene

## Understand it

In improvisation, anything your scene partner says or does is an **offer**. The core rule is **"yes, and"**: accept the offer (*yes*) and add something to it (*and*).

- Partner: "Doctor, my leg has turned blue!"
- Blocking: "No it hasn't." — the scene dies.
- Yes, and: "Hmm, and it's glowing slightly. Have you eaten anything strange this week?" — the scene grows.

**Blocking** (refusing or ignoring offers) is the most common reason improvised scenes fail. So is **wimping** — accepting but adding nothing, leaving all the work to your partner.

![An offer (“Doctor, my leg has turned blue!”) can be blocked (“No it hasn't” — the scene dies) or accepted and built on with “yes, and” (“And it's glowing slightly…”), which grows the scene.](media:arts/yes-and.svg)

Other useful habits:

- **Make your partner look good.** Give them interesting offers to respond to.
- **Establish who, what and where early**: "Mama, the generator's off again and the customers are waiting!" tells us relationship, situation and place in one line.
- **Listen** — your next line comes from what they just said, not from a plan in your head.
- **Commit** fully to choices, even silly ones.

This is not only a game. Scripted acting works the same way: each line your partner says is an offer you must actually receive and react to. Actors who only wait for their cue look wooden; actors who say "yes, and" to every moment look alive.

## Key words

- **Offer:** anything a partner says or does that the scene can build on
- **Yes, and:** accept the offer and add to it
- **Blocking:** rejecting or ignoring an offer
- **Who, what, where:** relationship, situation and place — established early

## Read and watch

- [GCSE Drama](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/subjects/zbckjxs) — BBC Bitesize
- [RSC education resources](https://www.rsc.org.uk/education) — Royal Shakespeare Company

## Practise at home

1. Play "yes, and" with a friend or sibling
1. Notice one real conversation where someone blocked an offer

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** Work on one short moment rather than the whole scene. A truthful ten seconds is worth more than a whole page rushed.
- **If you already can:** Play the same moment three different ways and say which is strongest and why.

Your instructor watches you do it and marks against this week's three objectives, two marks each. The written check below is worth one mark: this is a practical subject and it is marked like one.

lessons.title: Reading a script for action
lessons.summary: Finding what is happening underneath the words, and marking it.
objectives: You will mark the beats of a scene
You will find a line where a character changes tactic
You will read for action, not for feeling
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Read a short scene aloud twice
- Mark where the scene turns — where someone changes approach
- Write your objective above each beat

. **With an AI assistant —** ask it for the historical background of the play, then check one fact against the script itself. Anything the script contradicts, the script wins.

## Understand it

A script is like the top of an iceberg: the words are visible, but what is really happening is underneath. That hidden layer is the **subtext** — what characters mean, want or feel but do not say. "I'm fine" can mean "I'm furious", "I'm heartbroken" or "please ask me again".

![An iceberg: above the water the line “I'm fine”; below it the subtext — I'm furious, I'm heartbroken, please ask me again.](media:arts/subtext-iceberg.svg)

Reading a script for action:

1. **Read the whole play** (or scene) more than once, before deciding anything.
2. **Gather the given circumstances** — facts the script states: where, when, who, what has just happened, relationships. Write them down.
3. **Find each character's objective** in the scene.
4. **Divide the scene into units (beats)** — a new beat begins whenever the topic, tactic or situation changes. Draw a line in the script at each change.
5. **Name the action** for each of your lines with an action verb: *to warn, to tease, to comfort, to accuse*. Write it in pencil in the margin.
6. **Note the subtext** where the words and the meaning differ.
7. **Look for the turning point** — the moment the scene changes direction.

Marking the script in pencil (so you can change your mind) turns a page of words into a plan you can play. Directors and professional actors do exactly this before rehearsals begin.

## Key words

- **Subtext:** the meaning beneath the words
- **Given circumstances:** the facts of the situation the script provides
- **Beat (unit):** a section of a scene with one objective or tactic
- **Turning point:** the moment a scene changes direction

- [GCSE Drama](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/subjects/zbckjxs) — BBC Bitesize

lessons.title: Building a character
lessons.summary: Physicality, voice and one specific detail that makes a character a person.
objectives: You will change your walk and voice for a character
You will choose one specific physical detail
You will stay in it for a whole scene
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Change one thing: the centre of your walk, your pace, your pitch
- Choose one specific detail — a habit with the hands, a way of sitting
- Play a scene keeping it consistent throughout

## Understand it

A character becomes a person when the audience believes they have a life beyond the scene. Build them in layers:

**1. Facts from the script** — age, job, family, situation, what others say about them.

**2. Questions you answer yourself** — where did they grow up? What do they want most in life? What are they afraid of? What did they do this morning? Answers must fit the script; where the script is silent, choose things that help you play it.

**3. Physicality** — how they move. Try leading with a different part of the body: a proud character might lead with the chest, a curious one with the nose, a tired one with the feet. Change pace, posture and gestures. Rudolf Laban's movement qualities help: is their movement **heavy or light, quick or sustained, direct or indirect**?

**4. Voice** — pitch, pace, volume, accent and rhythm. A character's voice should come from who they are, not be a funny voice stuck on.

**5. One specific detail** — a habit, an object, a phrase they repeat: a market woman who counts change twice, a teacher who always taps the table. A single precise detail is more convincing than many vague ones.

![Five layers of a character: facts from the script, questions you answer yourself, physicality, voice, and one specific detail such as a market woman who counts her change twice.](media:arts/character-layers.svg)

Test the character by **hot-seating**: classmates ask you questions and you answer in character, instantly. Gaps in your answers show where to work.

## Key words

- **Characterisation:** building a believable character
- **Physicality:** a character's way of moving and standing
- **Hot-seating:** answering questions in character to explore them
- **Specific detail:** one precise trait that makes a character real

lessons.title: Back to the week 3 scene
lessons.summary: Returning to the earlier scene with everything learnt since, and seeing what has changed.
objectives: You will replay an earlier scene
You will name three things you now do differently
You will take a note and apply it immediately
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Play the week 3 scene again, unprepared
- Compare it with how you played it then
- Take one note and play it again straight away

## Understand it

In week 3 you played a scene using objective, obstacle and tactics. Since then you have learnt status, "yes, and", subtext and character building. Today you go back to the same scene and apply everything.

Work through it in layers:

1. **Re-read your week 3 notes.** Is the objective still the strongest? Often, with more understanding, a sharper objective appears.
2. **Mark the beats** and name an action verb for each line.
3. **Map the status** — who is high at the start, where it shifts, who ends higher.
4. **Add the subtext** — where are the words and the meaning different?
5. **Build the character** — physicality, voice and one specific detail.
6. **Play it with real listening** — receive each line as an offer and react.

Then **compare**. Many groups film both versions (with permission) and watch them side by side. Ask:

- What is clearer now?
- Where is the scene more alive, and why?
- What did you discover that you did not see in week 3?

This kind of return is how actors grow: the same material, revisited with more tools, reveals more each time. Professional actors play the same role for months and keep finding new things in it.

## Key words

- **Layering:** adding techniques one at a time to a performance
- **Revisiting:** returning to earlier work with new skills
- **Self-evaluation:** judging your own work honestly against criteria

- [GCSE Drama](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/subjects/zbckjxs) — BBC Bitesize

lessons.title: Listening and reacting
lessons.summary: Acting is mostly reacting, and reacting needs you to actually hear the other person.
objectives: You will react to what your partner does, not to what you planned
You will hold a silence
You will say why listening is most of acting
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Play a scene where you may not plan your next line
- Hold a three-second silence before answering
- Watch two classmates and name who is really listening

## Understand it

"Acting is reacting" is one of the oldest rules of the stage. Audiences often watch the person **listening**, not the person talking — because that is where the effect of the words shows.

Poor listening looks like: waiting for your cue, looking at the floor, preparing your next line, reacting the same way every night whatever your partner does. Good listening means actually **hearing** what is said — as if for the first time — and letting it change you before you reply.

Exercises that build it:

- **Repetition** (from the American teacher Sanford Meisner): two actors repeat a simple observation back and forth ("You're smiling." "I'm smiling."), letting the tone change only in response to what the other person really does.
- **Mirroring** — copy a partner's movements exactly, in real time, so neither seems to lead.
- **Pause before replying** in rehearsal: hear it, let it land, then answer. The pause can shrink later; the listening stays.
- **Do not plan reactions.** If you have decided to gasp at line 12, you will gasp whether or not your partner earns it.

On stage, real listening makes every performance slightly different, and that freshness is exactly what makes theatre live. It also rescues you: if a partner forgets a line, a listening actor notices at once and helps.

## Key words

- **Active listening:** really hearing and responding to your partner
- **Reaction:** the visible effect of what someone says or does
- **Meisner repetition:** an exercise in responding truthfully to a partner

lessons.title: Voice for the stage
lessons.summary: Being heard at the back without shouting, and being understood.
objectives: You will project using breath support
You will articulate consonants clearly
You will speak to the back of the room without strain
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Breath support: the sound carries on air, not on throat tension
- Tongue twisters for articulation
- Speak a speech to the furthest wall

## Understand it

On stage you must be heard and understood at the back of the room — without shouting, which strains the voice and sounds angry.

The four parts of a strong stage voice:

1. **Breath support.** Breathe low into the belly and lower ribs, not high into the chest and shoulders. Let the breath power the sound steadily. Exercise: breathe in for four, then hiss out evenly for ten, fifteen, twenty counts.
2. **Resonance.** Sound becomes fuller and carries further when it vibrates in the chest and face. Hum and feel the buzz on your lips and nose; then open into "mmm-ah".
3. **Projection.** Send the voice to a point at the back of the room, with energy and intention, rather than pushing from the throat. Think of throwing a ball to the last row.
4. **Articulation.** Clear consonants carry meaning further than loudness. Tongue-twisters ("red lorry, yellow lorry"; "unique New York") wake up lips and tongue.

![A strong stage voice in four parts: breath support from the belly, resonance in chest and face, projection to the back row, and clear articulation — without shouting.](media:arts/stage-voice.svg)

Also: slow down — nerves speed us up; **finish the ends of lines**, which beginners drop; and face the audience as much as the scene allows.

Look after your voice: drink water, warm up before shouting scenes, avoid screaming, rest it when it is tired. If you are hoarse for more than two weeks, see a doctor.

## Key words

- **Breath support:** using steady low breath to power the voice
- **Projection:** making the voice carry to the back without shouting
- **Resonance:** the vibration that makes the voice full
- **Diction:** clear pronunciation of words

lessons.title: Nigerian theatre
lessons.summary: Soyinka, Osofisan and the Yoruba travelling theatre, and what they ask of an actor.
objectives: You will name three Nigerian playwrights or companies
You will perform a speech from a Nigerian play
You will say one thing this tradition asks that naturalism does not
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Read about Wole Soyinka, Femi Osofisan and Hubert Ogunde
- Perform a short speech from a Nigerian play
- Discuss direct address, music and chorus as tools

## Understand it

Nigeria has one of the richest theatre traditions in the world, and Nigerian actors draw on it.

**The Yoruba travelling theatre.** From the 1940s, **Hubert Ogunde** and later companies such as those of **Kola Ogunmola** and **Duro Ladipo** toured towns with plays combining song, dance, drumming, mime and dialogue in Yoruba, drawing on history, myth (Ladipo's *Oba Koso*, about the god Sango) and everyday life. Many of these companies later moved into film and television — one of the roots of Nollywood.

**Wole Soyinka**, the first African to receive the **Nobel Prize in Literature (1986)**, wrote plays such as *The Lion and the Jewel*, *Death and the King's Horseman* and *Kongi's Harvest* — combining Yoruba ritual, music and poetry with sharp political satire.

**Femi Osofisan**, one of the next generation, wrote plays such as *Once Upon Four Robbers* and *Morountodun*, using storytelling, songs and direct address to the audience to question power and injustice.

![Nigerian theatre: Ogunde's touring company in the 1940s, Ogunmola and Duro Ladipo's Oba Koso, Soyinka's The Lion and the Jewel (1959) and Death and the King's Horseman (1975), Osofisan in the late 1970s, Soyinka's Nobel Prize in 1986, and the companies' move into film — a root of Nollywood.](media:arts/theatre-timeline.svg)

What this theatre asks of an actor:

- **Total performance** — speaking, singing, dancing and drumming as one.
- **Language** — the rhythm and poetry of Yoruba and of Soyinka's English, which must be spoken with full understanding.
- **Ritual and presence** — playing gods, kings and ancestors with weight and stillness.
- **Direct engagement** with the audience, who are part of the event.

## Key words

- **Travelling theatre:** companies that toured towns performing plays
- **Total theatre:** performance combining speech, song, dance and music
- **Satire:** using humour to criticise power or society

1. Watch one recorded Nigerian production

lessons.title: Rehearsal discipline
lessons.summary: Being on time, off book, warmed up and ready — the part that gets people re-cast.
objectives: You will be off book for your scene
You will arrive warmed up
You will take notes without arguing
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Full rehearsal: on time, off book, warmed up
- Take notes in silence, write them down, apply them next run
- Run the scene three times with notes between

## Understand it

Talent gets people noticed; **discipline** gets them cast again. Directors remember who made rehearsals easy and who made them hard.

The professional habits:

- **On time** means early — ready to start at the call time, not arriving then. Lateness wastes everybody's time, not only yours.
- **Off book by the deadline.** Learn lines when asked to. Holding a script stops you listening, moving or reacting. Learn them by understanding the scene, not just parrot-fashion: why does the character say *this* now?
- **Warmed up** — body and voice ready before rehearsal begins.
- **Prepared** — script marked, notes from last time applied.
- **Notes taken well.** When the director gives a note, write it down, say "thank you" and try it. Do not argue in the room; ask questions afterwards if needed.
- **Quiet and attentive** when not on stage — watch, learn, be ready for your entrance.
- **Respect for everyone** — fellow actors, crew, stage management. The show depends on all of them.
- **Safety** — follow fight and lifting instructions exactly; never improvise physical contact.

Line-learning techniques: write the first letter of each word; record the other parts and leave gaps for yours; walk while saying lines; learn in small chunks, then join them; test yourself from memory every day.

## Key words

- **Call time:** when you must be ready to start
- **Off book:** knowing your lines without the script
- **Notes:** a director's feedback after a run
- **Professionalism:** reliable, respectful behaviour at work

lessons.summary: Performing a prepared scene for an audience.
objectives: You will perform a prepared scene from memory
You will stay in it when something goes wrong
You will give a classmate one useful note
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Warm up, then perform your scene
- If something goes wrong, stay in it and keep going
- Watch two classmates and give each a specific note

## Understand it

Performance is where all the work meets an audience. Preparation turns nerves into energy.

**Before the day:**

- Run the scene many times until it is secure — lines, moves (**blocking**), entrances and exits.
- Do a full **run-through** in the space, with any props and costume, so nothing is new on the day.

**On the day:**

1. **Warm up** body and voice thoroughly.
2. **Focus** — a quiet moment to recall your character's given circumstances and what they want at the start.
3. **Breathe low.** Nerves make breathing shallow and speech fast; slow breathing calms the body.

**During:**

- **Listen and react** — play the scene, not the audience.
- **If something goes wrong** — a forgotten line, a dropped prop — stay in character and keep going. Audiences rarely notice mistakes that the actors do not show. Help your partner if they are stuck.
- **Hold for laughs** and reactions — wait for the audience before the next line.

**After:** reflect honestly. What worked? Where was the energy strongest? What would you change? What did the audience respond to?

Nerves never fully disappear, even for professionals — the energy is part of what makes live performance exciting. The aim is not to feel no fear, but to be prepared enough that fear cannot stop you.

## Key words

- **Blocking:** the planned moves of actors on stage
- **Run-through:** performing the whole piece without stopping
- **Stage presence:** the energy and focus that hold an audience's attention

lessons.title: Who does what backstage
lessons.summary: The roles that make a show happen, and why every one of them is needed.
objectives: You will name six backstage roles
You will say who is in charge during a performance
You will choose a role to follow this term
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Map the roles: stage manager, LX, sound, set, props, costume, crew
- Learn the rule: during a show, the stage manager runs it
- Choose the department you will follow

## Understand it

For every person the audience sees on stage, several work unseen to make the show happen. The main roles:

- **Director** — the overall vision; works with actors and designers.
- **Stage manager (SM)** — runs rehearsals and, during performances, runs the whole show from the prompt desk, calling every cue. The centre of communication.
- **Deputy and assistant stage managers (DSM/ASM)** — the prompt book, props, scene changes, backstage organisation.
- **Lighting designer and operator** — what light does in each moment, and pressing the buttons during the show.
- **Sound designer and operator** — music, effects and microphones.
- **Set designer and builders** — the physical world of the play.
- **Costume designer and wardrobe** — clothes, fittings, repairs, quick changes.
- **Props** — every object actors handle, found or made.
- **Front of house** — the audience's experience: tickets, ushering, safety, programmes.
- **Producer** — money, scheduling, venue and making the show possible at all.

![Backstage roles around the stage manager, who runs the show and calls every cue: director, lighting, sound, set and props, costume, front of house, producer, deputy and assistant stage managers.](media:arts/backstage-hub.svg)

Every role is needed because theatre is live: a missed cue, a missing prop or a costume that will not close changes the performance for everyone. Backstage work is a respected career with real skills — electrical, carpentry, sound engineering, organisation — that are valued well beyond theatre, in events, concerts, churches, television and conferences.

## Key words

- **Stage manager:** the person who runs the show and calls the cues
- **Cue:** a signal for a lighting, sound or scene change
- **Front of house:** everything on the audience's side of the stage
- **Crew:** the backstage team

lessons.title: The stage, and staying safe on it
lessons.summary: Stage geography, and the rules that stop people being hurt in the dark.
objectives: You will use stage directions correctly
You will name five hazards and how each is controlled
You will tape and run a cable safely
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Learn upstage, downstage, stage left and right — from the actor's view
- Walk the space and list the hazards: cables, edges, dark, height, heat
- Tape down a cable properly

## Understand it

**Stage geography** gives everyone a shared language for where things are. Directions are given **from the actor's point of view, facing the audience**:

- **Stage left** is the actor's left (the audience's right); **stage right** is the actor's right.
- **Downstage** is towards the audience; **upstage** is away from them (stages were once sloped upwards away from the audience — hence the words).
- **Centre stage** is the middle. Combine them: "downstage left", "upstage centre".
- **The wings** are the hidden sides; **the apron** is any part in front of the curtain line.

![A stage plan seen from above with the audience at the bottom: upstage at the back, downstage nearest the audience; stage left is the actor's left, which is on the audience's right; the wings are the hidden sides.](media:arts/stage-plan.svg)

*Stage left is the actor's left, which is the audience's right.*

**Staying safe** matters especially in theatre, where people work in the dark, at height, near electricity and heavy objects:

- **Trip hazards** — tape down cables and mark edges and steps with white or glow tape.
- **Working at height** — only trained people on ladders and towers, with someone footing the ladder; nothing in pockets that can fall.
- **Heavy and hanging objects** — lift with your legs, get help; never stand under something being raised.
- **Electricity** — check cables for damage, never overload sockets, keep liquids away.
- **Fire** — know the exits and extinguishers; keep exits clear; never block fire doors with set.
- **Blackouts** — stay still until the lights return or use a dimmed torch; mark positions.
- **Communication** — shout "Heads!" if anything falls; report hazards immediately.

## Key words

- **Stage left / right:** the actor's left / right, facing the audience
- **Upstage / downstage:** away from / towards the audience
- **Wings:** the hidden spaces at the sides of the stage
- **Glow tape:** luminous tape marking edges and positions in the dark

## Read and watch

- [Theatrecrafts glossary](https://www.theatrecrafts.com/) — Theatrecrafts.com
- [Working at height](https://www.hse.gov.uk/work-at-height/) — UK Health and Safety Executive

lessons.title: Lighting I: what light does
lessons.summary: Visibility, mood, focus and time — the four jobs of stage lighting.
objectives: You will name the four jobs of lighting
You will light a face so it can be read
You will change a mood with colour and angle
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Light one person from the front, the side and below — compare
- Add colour and see the mood change
- Learn why lighting from below reads as sinister

## Understand it

Stage lighting does four jobs:

1. **Visibility** — the audience must see the actors' faces. Everything else comes second.
2. **Mood** — warm amber light feels cosy or nostalgic; cold blue light feels night-time, sad or eerie; harsh white light feels clinical or tense; red feels dangerous or passionate.
3. **Focus** — light tells the audience where to look. A single spotlight on one actor in a dark stage is the strongest focus there is.
4. **Time and place** — the angle and colour of light suggest morning, midday, sunset, a fire, a window, moonlight.

The tools for doing it are the **qualities** of light a designer controls:

- **Intensity** — how bright.
- **Colour** — from coloured filters (gels) or colour-mixing LED lanterns.
- **Direction** — front light shows faces but flattens them; side light gives shape; backlight separates actors from the background; light from below looks unnatural and spooky.
- **Distribution** — hard-edged spots or soft washes, large areas or small.
- **Movement** — how changes happen: a slow sunset fade or a sudden blackout.

![Light from the front shows faces but flattens them, from the side gives shape, from behind separates the actor from the background, and from below looks unnatural and spooky.](media:arts/light-directions.svg)

Watch a performance, a concert or a church service and identify each job and each quality. Then sketch a simple lighting plan for a short scene: what light, from where, in what colour, and why.

## Key words

- **Wash:** light spread evenly over an area
- **Spot:** a focused, defined beam of light
- **Gel:** a coloured filter placed in front of a light
- **Backlight:** light from behind that separates performers from the background

lessons.summary: Hanging a lantern safely, pointing it where you want, and writing the cue down.
objectives: You will rig a lantern with a safety chain
You will focus it on a marked spot
You will write a cue sheet
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Rig: clamp tight, safety chain always, cable dressed
- Focus the lantern onto a marked position
- Write a cue sheet: cue number, what changes, on what line

. **With an AI assistant —** ask it to explain a lighting or sound term you met today, then check the explanation against the actual equipment in the room.

## Understand it

A stage light is called a **lantern** (or fixture). Getting it working is a three-stage job: **rig**, **focus** and **plot cues**.

**Rigging** — hanging the lantern on a bar:

- Only trained people work at height, with the equipment and the bar secured.
- Clamp the lantern firmly and always fit a **safety bond** (a steel wire or chain) around the bar, so it cannot fall if the clamp fails.
- Check cables for damage; plug into the correct circuit; tape and tie cables neatly.
- Never look directly into a lantern; they get extremely **hot** — use gloves.

**Focusing** — pointing and shaping the light:

- Aim it at the area it must light, with someone standing in the spot.
- Adjust size and edge (sharp or soft) with the lantern's controls; use **shutters** or **barn doors** to cut light off scenery or the audience.

**Cues** — the planned changes:

![Three stages: rig the lantern with a clamp and a safety bond, focus it on the area and shape it with shutters or barn doors, then plot cues with a number, a moment and a fade time, called “stand by… go”.](media:arts/rig-focus-cue.svg)

- Each change gets a **cue number**, recorded in the lighting desk and in the stage manager's **prompt book** with exactly when it happens ("on the word *goodbye*", "as she sits").
- A cue also has a **fade time** — how long the change takes.
- During the show, the stage manager calls: "Lighting cue 12 — stand by" … "Go."

Write every cue down. A show that lives only in someone's memory cannot be run by anyone else.

## Key words

- **Lantern / fixture:** a stage light
- **Safety bond:** a steel wire that stops a lantern falling
- **Focusing:** aiming and shaping a lantern's beam
- **Cue:** a recorded lighting change with a number and timing

lessons.body:
## What to do

- Patch mic to mixer to speaker and get sound
- Set gain first, then the fader — in that order
- Create feedback deliberately, then kill it

## Understand it

A sound system has a simple chain: **source → mixer → amplifier → speaker**.

- The **microphone** turns sound (air vibrating) into a small electrical signal. Other sources include a laptop or phone playing music.
- The **mixer** (desk) combines all the sources and lets you control each one's **level** (volume), **EQ** (tone — bass, middle, treble) and where it goes.
- The **amplifier** makes the signal strong enough to drive the speakers (many speakers now have amplifiers built in — "active" speakers).
- The **speakers** turn the signal back into sound.

**Feedback** — the loud squeal or howl — happens when a microphone picks up sound from a speaker, which sends it back through the system, louder each time round, in a loop. To prevent it:

![Sound flows mic → mixer → amplifier → speaker. Feedback is the loop when the speaker's sound returns into the mic; keep mics behind speakers and close to the mouth, and pull the fader down if it squeals.](media:arts/sound-chain.svg)

- Keep microphones **behind** the main speakers, and never point a mic at a speaker.
- Bring the mic **close to the mouth** (a hand's width), so you need less gain.
- Turn up slowly; do not set levels higher than needed.
- Turn off mics not in use.
- Use EQ to reduce the frequency that is ringing.

If feedback starts, **pull the fader down immediately**, then find the cause.

Also know your mics: **dynamic** mics (like the Shure SM58) are tough and handle loud voices; **condenser** mics are more sensitive; **lapel/headset** radio mics free the actor's hands.

## Key words

- **Signal chain:** the path sound takes from source to speaker
- **Mixer:** the desk that combines and controls sound sources
- **Feedback:** a squeal caused by a mic picking up its own speaker
- **Gain:** how much a signal is amplified

lessons.title: Sound II: running a show
lessons.summary: Levels, cues and playback, and keeping a show sounding the same every night.
objectives: You will run sound cues from a sheet
You will set levels at a soundcheck
You will keep a show file
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Soundcheck every mic before the audience arrives
- Run playback cues from a written sheet
- Write down your settings so tomorrow matches today

## Understand it

Running sound for a show means doing the same thing, the same way, every performance — so the audience on the last night hears what the director approved on the first.

**Before the show:**

- **Line check** — every mic and source working, every speaker sounding.
- **Sound check** with performers — set each mic's level and EQ so voices are clear and balanced. Note the settings.
- **Batteries** — fresh batteries in every radio mic, every show (a dying battery causes crackles and drop-outs). Keep a log.
- **Playback** — music and effects in order, at the right levels, ideally in show software (such as QLab or a cue list) rather than scrolling through a phone.

**During the show:**

- Follow the **cue sheet**: each cue's number, what it is, when it happens, its level and fade.
- Respond to the stage manager's calls: "Sound Q7, stand by… Go."
- **Ride the faders** — bring each actor's mic up when they speak and down when they do not, to reduce noise and feedback.
- Wear headphones to check, but judge the mix by what the audience hears.

![A sound cue sheet listing each cue's number, what it is, the moment it happens, its level and its fade — so anyone could run the show the same way.](media:arts/cue-sheet.svg)

**After:** note any problems for tomorrow, charge or change batteries, store mics safely.

Consistency is the professional standard: write down every setting, so anyone could run the show the same way.

## Key words

- **Sound check:** testing and setting levels with performers
- **Cue sheet:** the list of sound cues with timings and levels
- **Playback:** playing recorded music and effects in a show
- **Riding the faders:** adjusting levels live as people speak

lessons.title: The safety walk again, with the rig live
lessons.summary: Returning to the week 2 hazard walk now that there are cables, lanterns and heat in the room.
objectives: You will repeat the earlier hazard walk on a rigged stage
You will find hazards that did not exist in week 2
You will fix three of them
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Walk the space again with the rig in and the lights on
- List what is new: heat, trailing cable, dark edges, working at height
- Fix three hazards yourself

## Understand it

In week 2 you did a hazard walk on an empty stage. Now the space has a lighting rig, sound equipment, cables, and lanterns that run hot — the risks have changed, so you walk it again.

A **risk assessment** asks for each hazard: *who could be harmed, how, how likely, how bad, and what control reduces it?* Walk the space methodically — stage, wings, backstage, control position, audience area — and look for:

- **Cables** — across walkways (cover or tape them), damaged insulation, overloaded extension leads and daisy-chained adaptors.
- **Heat** — lanterns near curtains, set or costumes (fire risk); hot lanterns at head height; ventilation.
- **Height** — anything rigged must be bonded; ladders stored safely; nothing loose on bars.
- **Electricity** — water near equipment, missing covers, unknown wiring. Only competent people work on electrics.
- **Movement in darkness** — edges, steps and set pieces marked; clear routes for scene changes and exits.
- **Fire exits** — clear, signed and lit; extinguishers present and their type known.
- **Weight** — set pieces stable and braced; heavy items stored low.

Record each hazard, the control and who is responsible. Fix what you can at once; report what you cannot. Repeat the walk whenever the space changes — and before every performance.

## Key words

- **Risk assessment:** identifying hazards and how to reduce them
- **Hazard:** something that could cause harm
- **Control measure:** an action that reduces a risk
- **Daisy-chaining:** plugging extension leads into each other — a fire risk

lessons.title: Set and props, cheaply
lessons.summary: Building what the story needs from what you can actually get.
objectives: You will build a simple set piece safely
You will source props without spending much
You will say why a prop must be reliable
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Build a flat or a rostrum safely, with supervision on tools
- Source three props from what the centre already has
- Test every prop that an actor must handle

## Understand it

Set and props tell the audience where they are and who the characters are. On a small budget, the skill is **selection**: give the audience only what the story truly needs, and let their imagination do the rest.

Start from the script:

- List every prop actors **use** (a phone that rings, a bowl of rice served, a letter read) — these are essential.
- List what tells the audience **where and when** — often one strong piece does it: a market stall, a church bench, a single door.
- Cut everything else.

Making it cheaply:

- **Found and borrowed** items — chairs, crates, cloth, buckets. Keep a list of who lent what, and return it.
- **Recycled materials** — cardboard, plastic bottles, offcuts, pallets.
- **Fabric** transforms spaces: a wrapper becomes a curtain, a tablecloth, a river.
- **Paint** makes cheap things look right from a distance — stage scenery is designed to be seen from the audience, not up close.
- **Multi-use pieces** — a box that is a seat, a table and a car.

Practical rules: props must be **safe** (no real blades; stage weapons only under supervision), **sturdy** enough for every performance, and **kept on a props table** backstage with each item's place marked, checked before every show.

## Key words

- **Set:** the physical scenery of a production
- **Prop:** an object handled by actors
- **Props table:** a backstage table with marked places for each prop
- **Suggestion:** showing a place with a few chosen items, not a full replica

lessons.title: Costume and quick changes
lessons.summary: Dressing a character, and getting them changed in ninety seconds.
objectives: You will plan a costume for a character
You will run a quick change
You will set a change area
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Plan a costume from what the story says about the person
- Set a quick-change area: laid out, in order, lit
- Time a change and then make it faster

## Understand it

Costume tells the audience who a character is before they speak: age, wealth, job, personality, era and place. A crisp agbada, a faded school uniform, a market woman's wrapper and headtie — each tells a story.

Designing costume:

1. **Read the script** for each character's facts and changes.
2. **Make a costume plot** — a chart of every character, every scene and what they wear, showing every change.
3. **Think in silhouette and colour** — from the back row, shape and colour read more than detail. Colours can connect characters (families, groups) or contrast them.
4. **Source** from wardrobes, markets, borrowing and adapting. Keep labels with names.

![A costume plot grid of characters by scenes, showing what each wears and highlighting the scenes where a change happens.](media:arts/costume-plot.svg)

**Quick changes** — sometimes ninety seconds or less in the wings:

- Plan the change on paper: what comes off, what goes on, in what order, and where the dresser stands.
- **Pre-set** the costume in order, opened up and ready, on a chair or rail in the wings, marked with the character's name.
- Use quick fastenings — Velcro, poppers, elastic, zips — instead of many buttons.
- **Layering** — wear the next costume under the first where possible.
- **Rehearse** the change several times with the dresser until it is reliable.

Care: repair kit (needles, thread, safety pins) ready backstage; costumes hung, checked and washed between shows.

## Key words

- **Costume plot:** a chart of every character's costume in every scene
- **Quick change:** a fast costume change during a show
- **Dresser:** the crew member who helps actors change
- **Silhouette:** the overall shape of a costume seen from a distance

lessons.title: Stage management and the prompt book
lessons.summary: The book that holds the show: blocking, cues, and everything anyone needs to know.
objectives: You will build a prompt book page
You will record blocking
You will call a cue
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Set up the book: script on the right, cues and blocking on the left
- Record blocking in a shorthand you can read back
- Call a cue: standby, then go

## Understand it

The **prompt book** is the master copy of the production — the "bible" of the show — kept by the stage manager (or deputy). If anyone needs to know anything about the show, it is in the book, so that the show could be run by someone else if needed.

What it contains:

- **The script**, with wide margins, one page per sheet.
- **Blocking** — every actor's moves, written in pencil next to the lines, using stage directions and simple symbols.
- **Every cue** — lighting, sound, set changes, effects — marked exactly where it happens, with standby points before each.
- **Contact list** for the whole company.
- **Rehearsal schedule** and reports.
- **Prop list, costume plot and set changes.**
- **Show reports** — after each performance: running time, problems, audience notes.

![A prompt-book page: the script in the middle, the actors' blocking in pencil in the left margin (X DSL = cross downstage left), and each cue with its standby in the right margin.](media:arts/prompt-book.svg)

Calling cues: the stage manager speaks to operators on a headset. A standby is given before each cue ("Standby lighting cue 14, sound cue 6"), the operators confirm ("Standing by"), and the cue is triggered with **"Go"** at the exact moment ("LX 14 and sound 6… go"). The word *go* is only used to start cues.

Use pencil (blocking changes constantly in rehearsal), keep it neat enough for anyone to read, and never let it leave the building without a copy.

## Key words

- **Prompt book:** the master copy of the show with blocking and cues
- **Standby:** the warning given before a cue
- **Show report:** the record of each performance
- **Calling:** giving cues to operators during the show

lessons.title: The technical rehearsal
lessons.summary: Running the show for the technical elements, slowly, and fixing what breaks.
objectives: You will work through a tech rehearsal in order
You will stop, fix and go back cleanly
You will keep a list of what still needs fixing
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Run the show cue by cue, stopping whenever needed
- Learn how to go back: "from the top of the scene"
- Keep a running list of outstanding jobs

## Understand it

The **technical rehearsal** ("tech") is where all the technical elements — lights, sound, set, costume changes and props — are put together with the actors for the first time. It is slow, detailed and essential.

How it runs:

- Work through the show **cue by cue**. Actors play only the moments around each cue ("cue to cue"), skipping long scenes without technical changes.
- At each cue, check: does it happen at the right moment? At the right level and speed? Can everyone see and hear? Is the change safe?
- **Stop and fix** problems immediately — reposition a lantern, re-time a fade, re-plan a scene change.
- The stage manager updates the prompt book with every change.

![Across the running time of a show, only the short stretches around each cue are played in a cue-to-cue technical rehearsal; long scenes with no technical change are skipped.](media:arts/cue-to-cue.svg)

After the tech come **dress rehearsals** — the full show, in costume, at performance speed, ideally without stopping, as if an audience were there.

Good tech habits:

- **Patience** — it often takes many hours. Everyone stays focused and quiet on stage when a problem is being solved.
- **Clear communication** on headsets — short, calm and precise.
- **Safety** — scene changes in the dark are rehearsed slowly first; nobody moves set until it is safe.
- **Notes** — at the end, every department reports what still needs fixing, with an owner and a deadline before the next rehearsal.

## Key words

- **Technical rehearsal:** rehearsing all technical elements together, slowly
- **Cue to cue:** rehearsing only the moments around each cue
- **Dress rehearsal:** a full run in costume at performance speed

lessons.summary: Running a real performance in your department, start to finish.
objectives: You will run your department for a whole performance

lessons.body:
## What to do

- Run your department from the house opening to the end
- When something goes wrong, solve it quietly and keep going
- Reset and make safe afterwards — the show is not over until that is done

## Understand it

Running a real performance in your department brings together everything in the course. The show depends on preparation and calm.

**Before the audience arrives (the pre-show checks):**

- **Lighting** — every lantern working (a "rig check"), desk at the first cue.
- **Sound** — line check, fresh batteries, playback at the first cue.
- **Set and props** — everything in its pre-set position; props table checked against the list.
- **Costume** — quick-change stations pre-set; repair kit ready.
- **Safety** — walk the space: exits clear, cables secure, edges marked.
- **Stage management** — prompt book ready, headsets checked, cast called, house clearance given to front of house.

**During the show:** follow the prompt book; respond to standbys and "go"s exactly; stay alert for problems and solve them quietly; communicate calmly. If something goes wrong, the rule is: **the show goes on, safely**. A missed cue is fixed by taking it as soon as possible, not by panicking.

**After:** reset everything for the next show, write a show report (running time, problems, fixes needed), and thank your team.

Reflect: what went well in your department, what did you solve under pressure, and what would you prepare differently? Those are the skills events, concerts, broadcasters and churches hire for.

## Key words

- **Pre-show checks:** the checks every department makes before each performance
- **Rig check:** testing every lantern before a show
- **Show report:** the record of each performance
- **Reset:** returning everything to its starting position

lessons.title: A kitchen that does not hurt anybody
lessons.summary: Handwashing, knives, fire and hot oil — the four things that actually injure people.
objectives: You will wash your hands to the correct method
You will name the four main kitchen dangers and the control for each
You will put out a small oil fire correctly
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Learn the handwash: 20 seconds, between fingers, thumbs, wrists
- Walk the kitchen and name every hazard you can see
- Learn: an oil fire is smothered, NEVER watered

## Understand it

Every year, millions of people fall ill from food that looked and smelled fine. The World Health Organization sums up how to prevent it in **Five Keys to Safer Food**:

1. **Keep clean** — hands, surfaces and equipment. Wash hands with soap for at least 20 seconds before handling food, after the toilet, after touching raw meat, fish or eggs, and after handling rubbish or money.
2. **Separate raw and cooked** — raw meat, chicken and fish carry germs that spread to ready-to-eat food. Use separate boards and knives, or wash them thoroughly between uses; store raw below cooked.
3. **Cook thoroughly** — especially meat, chicken, eggs and seafood. Chicken juices must run clear, with no pink.
4. **Keep food at safe temperatures** — germs multiply fastest between about **5°C and 60°C**. Do not leave cooked food at room temperature for more than **two hours**; keep hot food hot and cold food cold.
5. **Use safe water and raw materials** — clean water, fresh ingredients, nothing past its date.

![A thermometer: food is kept cold at 5°C or below and hot above 60°C; between 5°C and 60°C is the danger zone where germs multiply fastest, so cooked food stays out no more than two hours.](media:arts/food-temperatures.svg)

The other half of kitchen safety is not hurting people:

- **Fire** — never leave hot oil unattended. If a pan of oil catches fire, **turn off the heat and cover it with a lid or damp cloth. Never throw water on it** — water turns to steam instantly and throws burning oil across the room.
- **Burns** — handles turned inwards; dry cloths for hot pans (a wet cloth conducts heat); cool a burn under running water for 20 minutes.
- **Gas** — smell gas? Turn it off at the cylinder, open windows, no flames or switches.
- **Slips** — wipe spills at once.

## Key words

- **Cross-contamination:** germs spreading from raw food to ready-to-eat food
- **Danger zone:** about 5–60°C, where bacteria multiply fastest
- **Food poisoning:** illness from eating contaminated food
- **Smother:** putting out a fire by cutting off its air

lessons.title: Knife skills and mise en place
lessons.summary: Holding a knife safely, the basic cuts, and having everything ready before the heat goes on.
objectives: You will hold a knife with a pinch grip and a claw hand
You will produce an even dice and an even slice
You will set out your mise en place before cooking
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Pinch the blade, curl the guiding fingers into a claw
- Practise dicing onion and slicing carrot evenly
- Lay out every ingredient prepared before any heat

## Understand it

**Mise en place** is French for "everything in its place". Before the heat goes on, every ingredient is washed, cut, measured and set out, and every tool is ready. Professional kitchens run on it, because once cooking starts there is no time to chop — the onions burn while you look for the pepper.

**Knife skills** make preparation fast, even and safe:

- **The grip** — pinch the blade between thumb and the side of the index finger, just in front of the handle; the other fingers wrap the handle. This gives far more control than holding only the handle.
- **The claw** — the guiding hand curls its fingertips under, with the knuckles forward. The flat of the blade rests against the knuckles, so the edge can never reach the fingertips.
- **The board** — stable (a damp cloth underneath stops it sliding), clean, and large enough.
- **A sharp knife is safer than a blunt one**: a blunt blade needs force, slips off the food, and cuts the hand.

Why cut evenly? Pieces of the same size **cook in the same time**. A mix of large and small dice gives a pot where some are mushy and some raw.

Basic cuts: **slice** (thin, flat), **dice** (cubes — onion is diced by cutting lengthways, then across), **chop** (rough pieces), **julienne** (matchsticks).

![Four cuts: slice (thin and flat), dice (even cubes), chop (rough pieces), julienne (matchsticks); even pieces cook in the same time.](media:arts/basic-cuts.svg)

Safety: never try to catch a falling knife; carry it pointing down beside your leg; never leave one in a washing-up bowl where nobody can see it.

## Key words

- **Mise en place:** having everything prepared and in place before cooking
- **Claw grip:** curled fingertips that guide food and protect the fingers
- **Dice:** cutting into even cubes
- **Julienne:** cutting into thin matchsticks

lessons.title: Heat: what each method does
lessons.summary: Boiling, frying, steaming and grilling, and choosing the right one.
objectives: You will cook the same ingredient three ways
You will say what each method does to texture and flavour
You will control the heat instead of leaving it at maximum
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Cook one vegetable boiled, fried and steamed; taste all three
- Learn why high heat browns and low heat softens
- Practise adjusting the flame mid-cook

## Understand it

Cooking is the controlled use of heat, and each method moves heat into food differently.

**Moist heat** (water or steam) — cooks no hotter than about 100°C, so food softens but does not brown:

- **Boiling** — fast bubbles; good for rice, yam, pasta. Vigorous boiling breaks delicate food.
- **Simmering** — gentle bubbles; for stews and soups, so meat becomes tender rather than tough.
- **Steaming** — food sits above water; keeps colour, shape and more vitamins (moi moi is steamed).

**Dry heat** (hot air, metal or oil) — reaches far higher temperatures, so the outside **browns**:

- **Frying** — shallow or deep in hot oil (around 170–180°C for deep frying). Puff puff, plantain, chicken.
- **Roasting and baking** — hot air in an oven.
- **Grilling** — direct radiant heat (suya).

Why browning matters: above about 140°C, sugars and proteins react (the **Maillard reaction**) and create the deep flavours and colours of fried plantain, toasted bread and grilled meat. That cannot happen in boiling water, which is why a stew whose meat is browned first tastes richer.

![Moist heat — boiling, simmering, steaming — cannot go above about 100°C, so food softens without browning; dry heat goes far higher; browning starts above about 140°C and deep frying is 170–180°C.](media:arts/heat-methods.svg)

High heat browns the outside fast but may leave the inside raw; low heat cooks through gently. Good cooks change the flame during cooking — high to brown or boil, low to simmer. Learn to read the pot: the sound of frying, the size of bubbles, the smell before burning.

## Key words

- **Simmer:** cook in liquid with small, gentle bubbles
- **Steam:** cook with the vapour from boiling water
- **Maillard reaction:** browning that creates flavour above about 140°C
- **Dry heat:** cooking with hot air, oil or metal rather than water

lessons.title: Rice: jollof and fried rice
lessons.summary: Getting rice right, which is the dish you will be judged on more than any other.
objectives: You will cook rice to the correct texture
You will build a jollof base
You will say why the water ratio matters
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Build the base: pepper, tomato, onion, reduced properly
- Measure the liquid — do not guess
- Cook, rest, and fluff before serving

## Understand it

Jollof rice is judged at every party in West Africa, and its quality comes down to a few controllable things.

**The base** — blended tomato, tatashe (red bell pepper), scotch bonnet and onion, fried in oil until it is **properly reduced**: the water has cooked off, the oil rises to the top and the sour, raw tomato smell becomes sweet. An under-fried base gives sour, wet jollof. This takes time — 20 to 30 minutes, stirring so it does not burn.

**The liquid ratio** — rice absorbs a set amount of liquid. Too much and it turns mushy; too little and it stays hard. **Measure** stock and rice with the same cup, and note what works for the rice you buy (parboiled long-grain is common and forgiving).

**Low and covered** — once rice and liquid are in, the heat goes low and the pot is covered (many cooks add foil under the lid to trap steam), so the rice steams evenly. Stirring breaks grains and releases starch; let it cook.

**The bottom** — a little smoky "party" flavour at the base is prized; burnt and bitter is not. Low heat controls it.

**Rest and fluff** — off the heat, rest covered for a few minutes, then fluff with a fork.

![Jollof in order: fry the blended base 20–30 minutes until the oil rises; add rice and stock measured with one cup; cook low, covered and unstirred; rest and fluff.](media:arts/jollof-order.svg)

Fried rice is different: the rice is cooked first, cooled (cold, dry rice fries without clumping), then fried quickly over high heat with vegetables, liver or chicken and seasoning. Cooked rice must be cooled quickly and refrigerated — rice left warm can grow bacteria that cause food poisoning.

## Key words

- **Reduce:** cook a sauce until water evaporates and it thickens
- **Ratio:** the measured proportion of liquid to rice
- **Parboiled rice:** rice partly boiled before milling, which holds its shape

lessons.title: Soups and stews
lessons.summary: Egusi, efo riro and the order ingredients go in.
objectives: You will build a stew in the correct order
You will season in stages and taste as you go
You will cook a leaf vegetable without destroying it
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Learn the order: oil, aromatics, protein, liquid, long-cooking, then leaves
- Taste at every stage and adjust
- Add the leaves at the end, briefly

## Understand it

Nigerian soups and stews — egusi, efo riro, okra, ofe onugbu, banga, ayamase — vary hugely, but most follow the same logic: **build flavour in layers, and add each ingredient at the moment it needs**.

A typical order:

![Soup order: oil warmed, aromatics fried, pre-boiled protein, stock, long-cooking thickeners such as egusi or ogbono, and leaves last for only a few minutes.](media:arts/soup-order.svg)

1. **Oil** heated (palm oil should warm, not smoke heavily — burnt palm oil is bitter).
2. **Aromatics** — onion, pepper, locust beans (iru), crayfish — fried to release flavour.
3. **Protein** — meat or fish, often pre-boiled with seasoning so it is tender and its stock can be used.
4. **Liquid** — the stock.
5. **Long-cooking ingredients** — egusi, ogbono, cocoyam paste for thickening — given time to cook through.
6. **Leaves last** — ugu, bitterleaf (washed), spinach (efo), uziza. Leaves need only a few minutes; long boiling turns them dark, soft and drains their colour and some vitamins.

**Taste at every stage** — salt, seasoning and pepper build up; it is easy to add more but impossible to remove. Taste with a clean spoon each time.

Why order matters: ingredients that need long cooking go in early; delicate ones late. Getting this wrong is why some soups have tough meat and grey leaves at the same time.

Food safety for stews: cool leftovers fast (shallow containers), refrigerate within two hours, and **reheat until piping hot** throughout — not once, then again and again.

## Key words

- **Aromatics:** ingredients like onion and pepper fried first for flavour
- **Stock:** liquid flavoured by cooking meat, fish or bones
- **Thickener:** an ingredient that gives body, like egusi or ogbono
- **Season to taste:** adjust salt and seasoning by tasting

objectives: You will make a swallow to a smooth consistency
You will judge the water ratio by feel
You will serve it at the right temperature
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Make eba and amala, watching the consistency
- Learn the feel of correct texture — it is judged by hand, not a recipe
- Serve hot, covered, shaped

## Understand it

"Swallow" — eba, amala, pounded yam, fufu, semo, tuwo — is judged almost entirely by **texture**: smooth, no lumps, the right firmness to be pinched and dipped. That is learnt by feel and eye, not by recipe alone.

What controls texture:

- **Water temperature** — garri for eba needs **properly boiling** water; warm water gives a raw, gritty, sticky result.
- **Ratio** — more garri or flour makes it firmer; customers differ (some want soft, some hard), so ask.
- **Technique** — sprinkle the flour or garri, let it absorb briefly, then **turn firmly** with a wooden spatula (omorogun), pressing out lumps against the side. Amala's yam flour is stirred vigorously over heat until it is smooth and stretchy.
- **Speed** — swallow sets as it cools; turn and serve without stopping.

![Eba in four steps: properly boiling water, sprinkle the garri and let it absorb, turn firmly with a wooden spatula pressing out lumps, then serve hot, wrapped and shaped.](media:arts/eba-method.svg)

**Serving well:**

- **Hot**, wrapped or covered (in nylon, foil or leaves, or in a covered bowl) so it does not form a skin.
- **Shaped neatly** — wet hands or a wet bowl give a smooth round.
- **Portions** consistent — weigh a few to learn what a portion looks like.

Sides — fried plantain (dodo), moi moi, salad, coleslaw — complete a plate. Plantain fries best when ripe (yellow with black spots) and cut on the diagonal for more surface to brown.

## Key words

- **Swallow:** a soft dough like eba or amala, eaten with soup
- **Consistency:** how thick, smooth or firm a food is
- **Portion:** the amount served to one person

lessons.summary: Returning to the week 2 cuts now that your hands know them, and adding pace without losing safety.
objectives: You will repeat the week 2 cuts faster and still evenly
You will keep the claw hand at speed
You will say what your hands do differently now
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Dice an onion against the clock, with the correct grip
- Stop the moment the claw hand slips — speed never beats safety
- Compare your cuts with week 2

## Understand it

Professional cooks dice an onion in well under a minute — but they reached that speed through **accuracy first**. Speed comes from a correct, repeated movement, never from rushing a wrong one.

This week's test has a rule: **the moment your claw grip slips, stop**. A cut finger costs far more time than a slow onion, and it ends your shift.

The efficient onion dice:

![An onion half from above: first cut lengthways towards the root without cutting through it, then cut across with the claw guiding, so even dice fall away; the root holds the layers until last.](media:arts/onion-dice.svg)

1. Halve the onion through the root; peel; leave the **root on** — it holds the layers together.
2. Lay it flat. Make vertical cuts lengthways towards the root, but not through it.
3. (Optionally) one or two horizontal cuts.
4. Cut across, claw guiding, and even dice fall away.
5. Discard the root.

Why it gets faster with practice:

- The **knife does the work** — a sharp blade in a smooth rocking or sliding motion, not chopping force.
- **The claw moves back steadily** with each cut, setting the thickness.
- **Your setup** — board stable, onion close, a bowl ready — removes wasted movement.

Compare your cuts with week 2: lay your dice side by side. Are they more even? Is your time better *and* your grip still correct? Keep a record of time and evenness each week; both should improve together.

## Key words

- **Root end:** the part of the onion that holds the layers together
- **Consistency of cut:** every piece the same size
- **Economy of motion:** removing wasted movement to work faster

lessons.title: Baking and small chops
lessons.summary: Chin chin, puff puff and the small chops people actually pay for.
objectives: You will mix a dough to the right consistency
You will fry at the correct oil temperature

lessons.body:
## What to do

- Make chin chin and puff puff doughs
- Test the oil before the batch goes in — too cool makes it greasy
- Fry in batches so the oil stays hot

## Understand it

Small chops — puff puff, chin chin, samosa, spring rolls, buns — are a staple of Nigerian events, and frying them well is a skill that sells.

**The two doughs:**

- **Puff puff** is a **yeast** batter: flour, sugar, yeast, water (and nutmeg). Yeast feeds on sugar and gives off carbon dioxide gas, which makes the batter rise and the puff puff light. It needs warmth and time (about an hour) to rise, until doubled and bubbly. Too cold, or old yeast, and it stays flat and heavy.
- **Chin chin** is a firm, unleavened dough: flour, sugar, butter or margarine, egg, milk, nutmeg. Rubbed and kneaded, rolled thin and cut evenly, so every piece fries in the same time.

**Oil temperature is everything:**

![Oil too cool soaks into the food and leaves it greasy; at roughly 170–180°C a test drop sizzles and rises and browns in a minute or two; too hot burns the outside while the inside stays raw.](media:arts/oil-temperature.svg)

- **Too cool** — the food soaks up oil before it cooks, coming out greasy and heavy.
- **Too hot** — the outside burns before the inside cooks; puff puff stays raw inside.
- **About right** (roughly 170–180°C) — test with a small drop of batter: it should sizzle at once and rise to the top steadily, browning in a minute or two.

**Fry in batches**: too much food at once drops the oil temperature, and everything goes greasy. Let the oil recover between batches. Drain on paper or a rack.

Safety: dry hands and utensils (water spits violently in hot oil), lower food in gently away from you, never leave the pot, and keep a lid nearby.

## Key words

- **Yeast:** a living raising agent that makes dough rise with gas
- **Leavened:** made to rise with yeast or baking powder
- **Batch frying:** frying in small amounts so the oil stays hot

lessons.title: What a dish actually costs
lessons.summary: Buying, portioning, and knowing whether you made money.
objectives: You will cost a dish per portion
You will set a price that covers cost plus margin
You will say what you forgot to include the first time
lessons.body:
## What to do

- List every ingredient and what it cost
- Divide by portions to get cost per plate
- Add gas, packaging, transport and your time — most people forget these

. **With an AI assistant —** ask it to lay out a costing sheet for your dish, then do the arithmetic by hand on three rows. It gets structure right more reliably than numbers.

## Understand it

Many food businesses fail not because the food is bad but because they **do not know what a plate costs**, and price below it.

**Food cost per portion:**

1. List every ingredient in the recipe, including oil, seasoning and salt.
2. Find what you actually paid for each (for the whole bag, tin or kilo).
3. Work out how much of each the recipe uses, and its cost.
4. Add it up, then **divide by the number of portions**.

Example: a pot of jollof costing ₦15,000 in ingredients that serves 20 costs **₦750 a plate in food**.

**What people forget:**

- **Gas or charcoal** — measure how long a cylinder lasts.
- **Packaging** — plates, takeaway packs, nylon, spoons, serviettes. Often ₦200–₦500 a plate.
- **Transport** — to market and to the event.
- **Waste** — some food burns, spoils or is left over.
- **Your time** — hours of shopping, cooking, serving and cleaning, at a real rate. If you do not pay yourself, you have a hobby, not a business.

**Setting a price:** total cost per plate plus a **margin** (profit). Also check what others charge — but never price below your cost to compete.

![An example plate: food ₦750 (a ₦15,000 pot for 20), packaging ₦300, gas ₦100, transport ₦50, waste ₦75 and your time ₦250 — a cost of ₦1,525 before a margin, so a price of about ₦2,000.](media:arts/plate-cost.svg)

Ingredient prices change fast with inflation; re-cost your menu regularly.

## Key words

- **Cost per portion:** total cost divided by the number of portions
- **Overheads:** costs other than ingredients, like gas and packaging
- **Margin:** the part of the price above cost — the profit
- **Food cost:** the ingredients' share of a dish's cost

## Read and watch

- [Small business support](https://www.smedan.gov.ng/) — SMEDAN (Small and Medium Enterprises Development Agency of Nigeria)
- [Cooking techniques (videos)](https://www.bbc.co.uk/food/techniques) — BBC Food

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** Do one step at a time and finish it before starting the next. Most kitchen accidents happen when someone is rushing two jobs at once.
- **If you already can:** Cook the dish for twice the number of people, cost it, and teach one step to a classmate.

lessons.title: Plating and presentation
lessons.summary: Making food look like something someone would pay for.
objectives: You will plate a dish with deliberate placement
You will keep the plate rim clean
You will photograph a dish in good light
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Plate with height, colour contrast and space — do not fill the plate
- Wipe the rim before it leaves the kitchen
- Photograph in daylight, from above and at an angle

## Understand it

People eat with their eyes first, and in a business they also order from photos. **Plating** is the arrangement of food so it looks as good as it tastes.

Principles used by professional chefs:

![A plate seen from above: rice shaped for height, the protein at the front as the focal point, three pieces of plantain, a green for colour contrast, empty space, and a clean wiped rim.](media:arts/plating.svg)

- **Space** — do not cover the plate. Leave clean rim and some empty space; a crowded plate looks cheap.
- **Height** — build up rather than spread flat: rice shaped with a ring or cup, protein leaning against it.
- **Colour contrast** — jollof, green vegetables, golden plantain and a slice of tomato look alive; a plate of only brown looks dull. Use garnish that is **edible and belongs to the dish**.
- **Odd numbers** — three pieces of plantain look more natural than two or four.
- **A focal point** — the protein, usually placed at the front or centre.
- **Clean rims** — wipe drips with a clean cloth before the plate leaves. A smear looks careless.
- **Hot food on warm plates**, cold food on cold.

**Photographing food:**

- **Daylight** from a window, from the side — never a direct flash.
- Choose the angle: **from above** for flat dishes and spreads; **from the side (about 45°)** for height.
- A plain background; clean surroundings.
- Take it immediately — food dulls quickly.
- Never photograph food you are not selling as if you are.

## Key words

- **Plating:** arranging food attractively on a plate
- **Garnish:** an edible addition for colour and finish
- **Focal point:** where the eye goes first on the plate

## Read and watch

- [Cooking techniques (videos)](https://www.bbc.co.uk/food/techniques) — BBC Food
- [Five keys to safer food manual](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241594639) — World Health Organization
