lessons.title: Catering an event
lessons.summary: Quantities, timing and the order of work when you are cooking for forty.
objectives: You will calculate quantities for a given number
You will write a timed plan working backwards from service
You will say what must be cooked last
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Scale a recipe from 4 to 40 and check the quantities make sense
- Write a timeline backwards from the serving hour
- Decide what can be done the day before and what cannot

## Understand it

Cooking for 40 is not cooking for 4 ten times. Three things change: **quantity, time and safety**.

**Scaling recipes:**

- Find the **scaling factor**: 40 ÷ 4 = **10**. Multiply each ingredient.
- **Check that it makes sense.** Salt, pepper and strong seasoning often need less than full multiplication — add gradually and taste. Liquid can need adjusting because large pots lose less water to evaporation.
- **Equipment** — will it fit? You may need several pots or batches.

**The timeline — work backwards from serving time:**

![A backward timeline from 2 pm service: plating starts at 1:30, jollof at 11:30 (an hour), the base at 10:50 (40 minutes before), and shopping and boiling the meat the day before.](media:arts/event-timeline.svg)

- Serving at 2 pm? Plating starts at 1:30. Jollof needs 1 hour from start; the base needs 40 minutes before that. Meat must be boiled first. Shopping is the day before.
- Write each task with a start time, and what can be **done ahead** (shopping, washing, chopping, boiling meat, making the base) and what must be **done on the day** (rice, frying, salad).

**Food safety at scale** — the risks multiply:

- Large pots cool slowly; divide food into **shallow containers** to cool fast, and refrigerate within 2 hours.
- **Hot holding** — keep served food hot (above 63°C) in covered food warmers.
- Food left out at an event for over 2 hours should be thrown away.
- Clean hands, clean serving spoons, and food covered against flies.

Allergies: ask clients about guests' allergies (nuts, shellfish, eggs) and **label dishes** clearly.

## Key words

- **Scaling factor:** the number you multiply a recipe by
- **Backward timeline:** a plan made from the serving time backwards
- **Hot holding:** keeping cooked food hot (above 63°C) until served
- **Allergen:** an ingredient that causes an allergic reaction

## Read and watch

- [Safer food, better business](https://www.food.gov.uk/business-guidance/safer-food-better-business) — UK Food Standards Agency
- [Allergen guidance for food businesses](https://www.food.gov.uk/business-guidance/allergen-guidance-for-food-businesses) — UK Food Standards Agency
- [Food regulation in Nigeria](https://www.nafdac.gov.ng/) — NAFDAC

## Practise at home

1. Write a full plan for feeding your family plus ten guests
1. Scale one recipe up and check the maths twice

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** Do one step at a time and finish it before starting the next. Most kitchen accidents happen when someone is rushing two jobs at once.
- **If you already can:** Cook the dish for twice the number of people, cost it, and teach one step to a classmate.

lessons.title: Cook and serve a meal
lessons.summary: A full meal, planned, costed, cooked to time and served.
objectives: You will plan, cost and cook a two-course meal
You will serve it on time
You will keep the kitchen safe and clean throughout
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Cook and serve your planned meal to the class or to guests
- Hold your timings — serve hot food hot
- Clean down as you go; the job is not finished until the kitchen is

## Understand it

This is a full service — the same job a caterer does for a client.

**Before:** your shopping list, costed menu, prep list and backward timeline are done. Everyone in the team knows their station and their tasks.

**During — what a professional service looks like:**

- **Mise en place** complete before cooking.
- **Timings held** — hot food served hot, cold food cold, everything ready together.
- **Clean as you go** — wipe surfaces, wash tools between tasks, take out rubbish. A cluttered station is slow and unsafe.
- **Communication** — call out "hot pan behind!", "knife!", "ready to plate".
- **Taste** before anything leaves the kitchen.
- **Plating** to the standard you set, consistently, plate after plate.
- **Hygiene** — hand washing, separate raw and cooked, food covered.

**After:** the job is not finished until the kitchen is clean: equipment washed and stored, surfaces sanitised, floors swept, rubbish out, leftovers cooled and stored or discarded safely.

**Reflect honestly:**

- Did the food match the plan? Was the timing right?
- What did guests say? (Ask — feedback is free market research.)
- What did it really cost, against your costing?
- What would you change next time?

Record it all. A caterer's best tool is a notebook of what worked.

## Key words

- **Service:** the period of cooking and serving food to guests
- **Clean as you go:** cleaning continuously while working
- **Station:** one person's work area and set of tasks

## Read and watch

- [Safer food, better business](https://www.food.gov.uk/business-guidance/safer-food-better-business) — UK Food Standards Agency
- [Cleaning](https://www.food.gov.uk/safety-hygiene/cleaning) — UK Food Standards Agency

lessons.title: What adire is, and whose it is
lessons.summary: Indigo-resist cloth from Egbaland, the women who made it, and what the patterns mean.
objectives: You will say what resist dyeing means
You will name the three adire techniques
You will name two traditional motifs and their meanings
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Learn the word: adire means "tie and dye" in Yoruba — cloth that resists the dye in places
- Meet the three techniques: oniko (tied), alabere (stitched), eleko (paste)
- Look at olokun and ibadandun motifs and learn what they say

```swatch #f5f1e6 Undyed cloth | #6b7fb3 One dip | #35497e Three dips | #1b2545 Full depth
```

## Understand it

**Adire** (Yoruba: *adi* "to tie", *re* "to dye") is indigo-dyed cloth made by Yoruba women, especially in **Abeokuta** and **Ibadan**, where it became a major industry from the early twentieth century. All adire is **resist dyeing**: something is placed on or into the cloth to stop the dye reaching parts of it, and those parts stay pale when the cloth is dipped.

The three main techniques:

![Resist dyeing: where cloth is tied (oniko), stitched (alabere) or pasted with cassava starch (eleko), indigo cannot reach, so those areas stay pale against the blue.](media:arts/resist-principle.svg)

- **Oniko** — *tied*. Seeds, stones or folds are bound tightly with raffia; the binding resists the dye, leaving circles, rings and lines.
- **Alabere** — *stitched*. Lines of stitching (with raffia or thread) are pulled tight before dyeing and removed after, leaving fine lines and patterns.
- **Eleko** — *paste*. A starch paste made from cassava (**lafun**) is painted freehand or pressed through a **stencil** (traditionally zinc sheet). The paste resists the dye, and is washed out after.

**Whose craft is it?** Adire was historically women's work: dyers (**alaro**) who kept the indigo vats, and designers who painted eleko, with men cutting many of the stencils. Patterns carried names and meanings, and the knowledge was passed down in families and compounds.

Today adire is worn, exported and celebrated in fashion — and is also widely copied as cheap factory prints. Learning the real techniques, and naming the tradition when you sell or show your work, respects the women who built it.

## Key words

- **Adire:** Yoruba resist-dyed indigo cloth
- **Resist:** anything that stops dye reaching part of the cloth
- **Oniko / alabere / eleko:** tied / stitched / paste resist
- **Alaro:** a dyer who keeps an indigo vat

## Read and watch

- [Search the collections: adire](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/search/?q=adire) — Victoria and Albert Museum
- [Search: adire](https://artsandculture.google.com/search?q=adire) — Google Arts & Culture
- [Art of Africa](https://www.khanacademy.org/humanities/art-africa) — Khan Academy

## Practise at home

1. Find and photograph one adire cloth near you
1. Draw one traditional motif from memory

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** Work on a small sample square before you touch a full wrapper. A fold that fails on a 20cm square costs you nothing.
- **If you already can:** Combine two resist techniques on one cloth, and record your dye times so the result can be repeated.

## Assessed this week

lessons.title: Setting up safely
lessons.summary: Dye is a chemical. Gloves, ventilation, and a work area that protects you and the room.
objectives: You will set up a dye area with ventilation and covered surfaces
You will wear gloves, apron and eye protection correctly
You will say what to do if dye gets in an eye
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Cover every surface; work outdoors or by an open window
- Gloves, apron, goggles — on before the lid comes off
- Learn the rule: dye in the eye means rinse with clean water for 15 minutes and tell an adult immediately

## Understand it

Natural indigo is fairly gentle, but most modern dye workshops also use **chemicals** — caustic soda (sodium hydroxide), **sodium hydrosulfite** (a reducing agent), synthetic indigo, reactive dyes and fixers. Several of these are hazardous: caustic soda burns skin and eyes; dye powders can be breathed in; reducing agents give off fumes and can react with water or heat.

The workshop rules:

- **Read the label and the instructions** for every product before opening it. Labels carry hazard symbols — learn them.
- **Protective equipment on first**: gloves (rubber or nitrile), apron, and **goggles** when mixing or handling powders and caustic solutions.
- **Ventilation** — work outdoors or by open windows; mix powders where there is no wind to blow them at you; wear a dust mask for powders.
- **Add chemical to water, never water to chemical** — adding water to caustic soda can make it boil and spit.
- **Cover surfaces**; keep food and drink out of the dye area. Never use dye pots for cooking afterwards.
- **Label every container** with what it holds.
- **Spills** — clean up at once.

![Caustic soda is added slowly to water, never water poured onto it, which can boil and spit; gloves, apron and goggles first, good ventilation, and 15 minutes of running water for a splash in the eye.](media:arts/chemical-to-water.svg)

**First aid:** splashes in the eye — **rinse with clean running water for at least 15 minutes** and get medical help; on skin — remove contaminated clothing, rinse with plenty of water.

**Disposal** — do not pour strong caustic or dye waste into streams or onto soil near water; neutralise and dilute as the product instructions say.

## Key words

- **Hazard symbol:** a label picture warning of a chemical's danger
- **PPE:** personal protective equipment — gloves, goggles, apron
- **Caustic:** able to burn skin and eyes
- **Reducing agent:** a chemical that makes indigo soluble in the vat

## Read and watch

- [Hazardous substances (COSHH)](https://www.hse.gov.uk/coshh/) — UK Health and Safety Executive
- [Health and safety guidance](https://www.hse.gov.uk/) — UK Health and Safety Executive

## Practise at home

1. Set out a safe work area at home and have it checked
1. Learn the rinse rule by heart

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** Work on a small sample square before you touch a full wrapper. A fold that fails on a 20cm square costs you nothing.
- **If you already can:** Combine two resist techniques on one cloth, and record your dye times so the result can be repeated.

lessons.title: Adire oniko: tying
lessons.summary: Raffia and thread resist — the technique that makes rings, spirals and stars.
objectives: You will tie three different oniko resists
You will tie tightly enough to actually resist
You will predict the pattern before you dye
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Tie a stone or seed into the cloth and bind it tightly with raffia
- Try three bindings: single point, row of points, spiral
- Draw what you think the pattern will be before dyeing

## Understand it

In **oniko** (tie resist), the pattern comes from **pressure**: wherever the cloth is tightly bound, dye cannot get in. The tighter the binding, the sharper and paler the resist.

The classic bindings:

- **Single point** — pinch up a point of cloth (or wrap it round a seed or small stone), bind tightly beneath it with raffia. Gives a circle with a ring.
- **Row of points** — the same, repeated in a line or grid. Traditional oniko cloths have hundreds of tiny tied circles, called *eleso* (seeds).
- **Spiral** — twist the cloth from a centre point into a flat spiral and bind it — gives radiating lines.
- **Folding and binding** — pleat the cloth in folds like a fan, then bind at intervals — gives stripes.

What changes the result:

- **Tightness** — loose binding lets dye creep in, giving a soft, blurry edge.
- **Width of binding** — a wide wrap gives a wide pale band.
- **Cloth** — cotton takes indigo well; synthetic fabrics do not.
- **Wet or dry** — damp cloth can be tied more tightly and dyes more evenly.

**Predict, then dye.** Draw what you think each binding will produce before it goes in the vat. Comparing the drawing with the result is how you learn to control the pattern rather than hope for it.

![Oniko bindings and their results: a single bound point gives a circle with a ring, a row of points a line of small circles, a spiral radiating lines, and fan folds bound at intervals give stripes.](media:arts/oniko-bindings.svg)

## Key words

- **Oniko:** tie-resist adire
- **Binding:** the raffia or thread wrapped round the cloth
- **Eleso:** small tied circles like seeds

## Read and watch

- [Search the collections: adire](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/search/?q=adire) — Victoria and Albert Museum
- [Search: adire](https://artsandculture.google.com/search?q=adire) — Google Arts & Culture

1. Draw your prediction for each

lessons.title: Adire alabere: stitching
lessons.summary: Needle and thread resist — the technique for lines, waves and fine repeats.
objectives: You will stitch a running-stitch resist and pull it tight
You will produce a straight line resist and a curved one
You will say how stitch spacing changes the pattern
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Running stitch along a marked line, then pull up tight and knot
- Try close stitches and wide ones, and compare
- Fold the cloth first to repeat a pattern

## Understand it

**Alabere** ("made with the needle") uses stitching as the resist. Lines of running stitch are sewn through the cloth, **pulled up very tight** so the cloth gathers into compressed pleats, and knotted. The gathers resist the dye; when the stitches are cut out after dyeing, delicate lines and patterns remain.

Technique:

![Alabere in four steps: mark the line, sew a running stitch, pull it up hard into tight gathers and knot it, then dye and unpick, leaving a fine pale line.](media:arts/alabere-steps.svg)

1. **Mark the design** lightly with chalk or pencil.
2. **Stitch** along the lines with strong thread or raffia — knot or leave a long tail at the start.
3. **Pull up hard** — the tighter the gather, the clearer the resist — and knot securely.
4. **Dye**, rinse, dry, and then carefully **cut and pull out** the stitches.

What changes the result:

- **Stitch length** — short stitches give fine, dotted lines; long stitches give bolder marks.
- **Spacing between rows** — close rows give dense texture; wide ones give bands.
- **Folding first** — fold the cloth and stitch through both layers to make **mirror-image** or repeating patterns in one go.
- **Machine stitching** — some modern alabere uses machine-stitched tucks for faster, sharper lines (sometimes called *adire alabere eleso*).

Alabere was often used for patterns with names such as **olosupa** (moon) and lines of leaves. Compare a close and a wide stitch on the same cloth — and write down which you prefer for what.

## Key words

- **Alabere:** stitch-resist adire
- **Running stitch:** a simple in-and-out stitch
- **Gathering:** pulling stitches tight to compress the cloth
- **Mirror pattern:** made by stitching folded cloth

lessons.title: Adire eleko: cassava paste, freehand
lessons.summary: Starch paste painted on by hand with a feather or a broom rib — the most skilled of the three.
objectives: You will mix cassava starch paste to the right consistency
You will paint a freehand motif
You will dry the paste fully before dyeing
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Cook the cassava starch to a smooth paste that holds a line
- Paint a motif with a feather quill or broom rib
- Let it dry completely — wet paste washes off in the vat

## Understand it

**Adire eleko** uses a starch paste as the resist, and it allows the most detailed, pictorial designs of any adire technique. Freehand eleko is traditionally the work of women artists who painted it from memory.

**The paste (lafun):** cassava starch is cooked with water, often with a little **alum** or copper sulphate added (traditionally) to help it set and resist, until it is **smooth and thick** — like toothpaste: thin enough to flow from a brush or quill, thick enough to hold a sharp line without spreading into the cloth.

**Painting:**

- The cloth is **stretched flat** and firm on a board or table.
- Designs are drawn freehand with a **feather quill**, a broom rib (*palm frond rib*), or a small stick.
- The paste must **penetrate the surface** — a skin on top that does not reach the fibres will let dye creep under.
- Usually only **one side** is pasted, so the reverse dyes more evenly — which is why eleko cloth has a clear "front".

**Drying is essential:** the paste must be **completely dry** before dyeing — wet paste dissolves in the vat and the resist fails, often smearing the whole design. Dry it flat in the sun or air.

![Eleko freehand: cook the cassava paste to a toothpaste thickness, paint it onto stretched cloth, dry it completely, then dip briefly and scrape and wash the paste off to reveal the pale design.](media:arts/eleko-steps.svg)

**Dyeing:** dip carefully and briefly (paste softens if soaked for long). After dyeing and drying, the paste is **scraped and washed off**, revealing the pale design. The slight cracking of dried paste lets in fine veins of blue — a mark of hand-made eleko.

## Key words

- **Eleko:** paste-resist adire
- **Lafun:** cassava starch used to make the paste
- **Penetration:** paste soaking into the fibres, not sitting on top
- **Crackle:** fine veins where dye enters cracks in dried paste

lessons.title: Eleko with stencils
lessons.summary: Cut zinc or card stencils for repeating a motif accurately across a whole cloth.
objectives: You will cut a stencil
You will apply paste through it evenly
You will register a repeat across the cloth
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Cut a simple motif from zinc sheet or stiff card
- Spread paste through it with a flat blade, evenly
- Mark registration points so the repeat lines up

## Understand it

From the 1920s onward, stencilled eleko became common because it is **faster** and **repeatable**: a design cut once can be printed again and again. Traditionally, stencils were cut from **zinc** (from tea chests or roofing sheets), often by men, and the paste spread by women.

**Cutting a stencil:**

- Use stiff card (sealed with varnish or wax to resist the wet paste), acetate, or thin metal sheet.
- Draw a design with **bridges** — thin strips that hold the stencil together. A letter O cut out completely loses its middle; leave a bridge.
- Cut on a board with a sharp craft knife, cutting **away from your body**.

**Applying paste:**

- Lay the stencil flat on the stretched cloth; hold or weight it so it cannot shift.
- Spread paste **through** the stencil with a flat blade (a strip of metal or a spatula), in one or two firm, even strokes.
- Lift the stencil **straight up** to avoid smudging.
- Wash the stencil before the paste dries in it.

**Registration** — lining up repeats accurately:

![A stencil letter O cut with no bridges loses its middle; thin bridges hold it. Below, repeats line up edge to edge by matching small registration marks at the corners.](media:arts/stencil-bridges.svg)

- Mark small **registration points** on the stencil corners and on the cloth (chalk marks, or a grid drawn lightly).
- Each new print lines up with the previous one's marks, so the repeat pattern flows without gaps or overlaps.

Stencilled eleko is crisper and more regular than freehand; freehand is more individual. Both are adire.

## Key words

- **Stencil:** a sheet with a cut-out design for printing
- **Bridge:** a strip that holds a stencil's shapes together
- **Registration:** lining up each repeat accurately
- **Repeat:** a design printed again and again in a pattern

lessons.title: Tying again, knowing what the dye does
lessons.summary: Returning to the week 3 tied samples now that you have seen how long a dip takes and how far dye creeps.
objectives: You will retie the week 3 resists with what you now know
You will compare the old and new samples
You will record the dye time that gave each depth
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Retie the three week 3 bindings, tighter and more deliberately
- Dye them and lay them beside the originals
- Write down the dip count and minutes for each shade

## Understand it

In week 3 you tied by trial. Now you know what the vat does, and the aim is **control**: being able to predict, and repeat, a result.

What you now understand about indigo:

- Dye only reaches cloth that is **open to it** — so tightness of binding is everything.
- **Each dip adds depth**: one dip gives pale blue, several give deep blue, many give near-black blue. The resisted areas stay pale, so **contrast increases with dips**.
- Indigo needs **air between dips** to oxidise; dipping again before it turns blue adds little.
- Dye **creeps** along damp fibres under a loose binding, softening the edge.

![Five swatches from one dip (pale blue) through two, four and six to many dips (near-black blue), each with a pale resisted square — contrast increases with every dip.](media:arts/dip-depth.svg)

The exercise:

1. Retie the three bindings from week 3 — single point, row, spiral — **tighter and more deliberately**.
2. Dye them with a **planned** number of dips and minutes.
3. Lay them beside the week 3 originals.

**Keep a dye log** — the professional habit that makes results repeatable:

- Date, cloth type and size.
- Binding or resist used.
- Number of dips, minutes per dip, minutes in air.
- The vat's condition (colour, smell, how long since it was fed).
- A small cut sample or photo of the result.

With a log, a result you love can be made again on purpose — the difference between a dyer and a lucky beginner.

## Key words

- **Dip:** one immersion of cloth in the vat
- **Oxidation:** indigo turning blue on contact with air
- **Dye log:** a record of every dyeing step and result
- **Contrast:** the difference between pale resist and dyed areas

1. Retie one sample a third time to confirm the result repeats

lessons.title: The indigo vat
lessons.summary: How indigo actually works — dipping, oxidising, and building depth one dip at a time.
objectives: You will dip and oxidise a sample correctly
You will build three depths of blue by dip count
You will explain why the cloth turns blue in the air
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Lower the cloth in gently — splashing adds oxygen and spoils the vat
- Lift it out and watch it turn from green to blue in the air
- Build depth with repeated short dips, not one long one

```steps 15 Prepare and check the vat | 10 Lower the cloth gently | 20 Oxidise in the air | 15 Second and third dips | 20 Rinse and unwrap | 10 Log the result
```

## Understand it

Indigo is unlike most dyes: it **does not dissolve in water**. To dye with it, the vat must be **reduced** — oxygen removed — which changes indigo into a soluble, yellow-green form called **leuco-indigo** ("white indigo") that can soak into fibres. Traditionally the alaro used fermented indigo leaves and alkaline wood-ash water; modern vats use a reducing agent and an alkali.

A healthy vat:

- Liquid is **yellow-green or amber**, not blue.
- A coppery, bronze-blue **"flower"** (froth) floats on top.
- It smells earthy.

**The magic of the dip:**

![In a healthy reduced vat the indigo is yellow-green; lifted out, the cloth turns green and then blue within a minute or two as oxygen fixes it; once fully blue, it is dipped again.](media:arts/indigo-dip.svg)

1. Lower the wet cloth in **gently and slowly** — no splashing, no stirring air in. Oxygen spoils the vat by turning the indigo blue (insoluble) before it reaches the cloth.
2. Keep it under for a few minutes, moving it gently below the surface.
3. Lift it out slowly, squeezing below the surface.
4. In the air it turns **green, then blue** within a minute or two, as oxygen locks the indigo into the fibres.
5. Wait until fully blue before the next dip.

**Building depth** — many short dips give deeper, more even, more lasting colour than one long one.

A vat "tires" as you use it (it turns blue, and the flower disappears); it must be **fed** (more reducing agent or alkali) and rested. Looking after a vat is the alaro's real skill.

## Key words

- **Reduction:** removing oxygen so indigo becomes soluble
- **Leuco-indigo:** the soluble yellow-green form of indigo
- **Flower:** the coppery froth on a healthy vat
- **Oxidation:** air turning the dye blue and fixing it in the fibre

1. Record the time and the result for each

lessons.title: Colour beyond indigo
lessons.summary: Modern dyes, how they differ from indigo, and keeping colour fast.
objectives: You will dye with a modern dye and fix it
You will compare fastness between two dyes
You will say what makes a colour run
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Dye a sample with a modern reactive dye and fix it as instructed
- Wash both an indigo and a modern sample and compare the water
- Learn what fixing does

## Understand it

Traditional adire is indigo blue; modern adire uses many colours, mostly from **synthetic dyes**.

The main families:

- **Natural dyes** — from plants and minerals: indigo (blue), camwood (*osun*, red-brown), kola nut (brown), onion skins (yellow-orange). Many need a **mordant** (often alum) to bind to the fibre.
- **Reactive dyes** — synthetic dyes for cotton that **chemically bond** with the fibre when fixed with an alkali such as soda ash. Bright, wide range of colours, very washfast when fixed properly.
- **Vat dyes** — like indigo, used in reduced form; very fast.
- **Direct dyes** — easy to use but wash out more.

**Fixing** is what makes a dye permanent:

![Indigo and other vat dyes fix by oxidising in air and are very fast; natural dyes like camwood need a mordant such as alum; reactive dyes fix with alkali, heat and time; direct dyes wash out more.](media:arts/dye-families.svg)

- Reactive dyes need the right **alkali, temperature and time** — follow the instructions exactly.
- Indigo fixes by oxidation in air, then washing.
- Unfixed dye **bleeds**: it runs in the wash, stains other clothes and fades fast.

**The wash test** this week: wash an indigo sample and a reactive sample separately in warm soapy water. Clear water means the dye is fixed; coloured water means loose dye is still coming out. Rinse until clear before selling anything — a customer whose new wrapper stains their white shirt does not come back.

Always check the **safety data** for synthetic dyes and fixers; wear gloves and a mask for powders.

## Key words

- **Mordant:** a substance that helps a natural dye bind to fibre
- **Reactive dye:** a synthetic dye that bonds chemically with cotton
- **Fixing:** making a dye permanent
- **Bleeding:** loose dye running out in the wash

lessons.summary: Traditional motifs, what they say, and designing your own with the same discipline.
objectives: You will draw three traditional motifs accurately

lessons.body:
## What to do

- Draw olokun, ibadandun and sunbebe from reference
- Design one motif of your own and write what it means
- Discuss: these patterns carried names, proverbs and status

. **With an AI assistant —** ask it what a traditional motif means — then check with an elder, a dyer or a museum record. It will invent Yoruba meanings that sound entirely convincing, and this is the exercise: find where it did.

## Understand it

Classic adire designs carry **names**, and many carry **stories, proverbs or commemorations**. A cloth could say something about its wearer, or record an event.

Some well-known patterns:

- **Olokun** ("goddess of the sea") — one of the most famous eleko designs, a grid of squares filled with many motifs, associated with wealth and the sea.
- **Ibadandun** ("Ibadan is sweet / pleasant") — celebrates the city of Ibadan, with motifs that include the pillars of **Mapo Hall**, a landmark of the city.
- **Sun mi n'mo** / **Sunbebe** — patterns whose names relate to closeness or to ornament (names and stories vary between dyers and towns).
- Patterns marking events — a coronation, a jubilee — so a cloth could carry history.

Motifs repeat within squares or bands: leaves, birds, combs, spoons, the moon, lizards, scissors — everyday and symbolic objects together.

**Designing your own motif:**

![Three ways a motif repeats: one motif per square in a grid of squares (as in Olokun), a band of motifs between plain areas, and an all-over grid edge to edge.](media:arts/motif-repeat.svg)

- Start from something meaningful to **you or your community**.
- Simplify it into a clear shape that works in one colour as a resist.
- Plan how it **repeats** — in a square, a band, a grid.
- Give it a **name**, and write what it means.

When you use a traditional pattern, name it and its origin. Adire patterns are part of Yoruba cultural heritage, and treating them as decoration with no source erases the women who created them.

## Key words

- **Motif:** a single design element that may repeat
- **Olokun:** a famous eleko pattern linked to the sea and wealth
- **Ibadandun:** a pattern celebrating Ibadan, including Mapo Hall
- **Heritage:** culture passed down from earlier generations

lessons.title: Finishing the cloth
lessons.summary: Washing out, drying, pressing — the steps that decide whether it looks professional.
objectives: You will wash out resist completely
You will dry without creasing or fading
You will press and fold for sale
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Wash out all paste and loose dye until the water runs clear
- Dry in shade, not direct sun — sun fades indigo
- Press and fold the cloth the way a seller would

## Understand it

The finish is what separates cloth people buy from cloth they hesitate over. Rushing it undoes weeks of work.

**Washing out:**

- Remove all bindings, stitches and remaining paste. Eleko paste softens with soaking, then is scraped off gently.
- Rinse in cool water, then wash with mild soap, then rinse again — **until the water runs clear**. Loose indigo rubs off on skin and clothes ("crocking"); a well-washed cloth does not.

**Drying:**

- **In the shade**, not direct sun — strong sun fades indigo over time and can leave uneven patches.
- Hang flat or straight so it dries without creases or drips leaving marks.

**Pressing:**

- Iron on the reverse while slightly damp, at the setting for cotton.
- **Beating** cloth with wooden mallets was traditionally used to give adire its glossy sheen.

**Presentation:**

![Finishing adire: wash out until the water runs clear, dry flat in the shade, press on the reverse while slightly damp, and label it with the technique, the pattern's name and care instructions.](media:arts/finishing-steps.svg)

- Fold the way a buyer wants to see it — so the **best part of the pattern** shows on top.
- Trim loose threads; hem or finish the edges.
- Attach a **label or card**: your name, the technique (oniko, alabere, eleko), the pattern name and its meaning, and **care instructions** — "Wash separately in cool water with mild soap. Dry in shade."

Care instructions protect the buyer's cloth — and your reputation.

## Key words

- **Crocking:** dye rubbing off onto skin or other cloth
- **Pressing:** ironing to remove creases
- **Care label:** washing and drying instructions for the buyer

lessons.title: Make and show a wrapper
lessons.summary: A full-size cloth, using at least two techniques, finished and presented.
objectives: You will produce a full wrapper using two techniques
You will present your dye log with it
You will price it honestly
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Make a full-size cloth combining two resist techniques
- Present it with your dye log so the result can be repeated
- Cost the materials and your time, and set a price

## Understand it

A full-size **wrapper** (about 2 yards / 1.8 m) brings together everything you have learnt, and is the scale real adire is sold at.

**Plan before you dye:**

![A full-size wrapper about 1.8 m long planned to scale: an oniko border of tied circles along top and bottom and an eleko stencilled panel in the centre — two techniques on one cloth.](media:arts/wrapper-plan.svg)

- Choose **two resist techniques** — for example eleko stencil in the centre with an oniko border, or alabere bands between plain areas.
- Sketch the full layout to scale. Think about how it will be worn: which parts show most when wrapped?
- Calculate materials: cloth, starch, thread or raffia, dye.

**Make it**, keeping your **dye log** at every step.

**Present it** with the log, so somebody else (or you, next year) could repeat the result.

**Cost it** honestly:

- **Materials** — cloth, dye, chemicals, paste, thread, gas or firewood, water.
- **Your time** — every hour of design, tying, stitching, pasting, dyeing, washing and finishing, at a fair rate. Hand-made adire can take days.
- **Overheads** — tools, gloves, transport, packaging.
- Add a **margin** for profit.

Compare the true cost with what factory "adire-print" sells for. Hand-made cloth cannot compete on price — it competes on **quality, authenticity and story**. Your label, your pattern's name and meaning, and your skill are why someone pays more.

## Key words

- **Wrapper:** a large rectangle of cloth wrapped as a skirt or dress
- **Layout:** the planned arrangement of the design on the cloth
- **True cost:** materials plus time plus overheads

## Read and watch

- [Small business support](https://www.smedan.gov.ng/) — SMEDAN (Small and Medium Enterprises Development Agency of Nigeria)
- [Search the collections: adire](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/search/?q=adire) — Victoria and Albert Museum

## Practise at home

1. Plan the design on paper first, full size
1. Test every technique on a sample before committing the cloth

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** Work on a small sample square before you touch a full wrapper. A fold that fails on a 20cm square costs you nothing.
- **If you already can:** Combine two resist techniques on one cloth, and record your dye times so the result can be repeated.

## Assessed this week

**Practical (6 marks) —** Produce a finished full-size adire wrapper using two techniques, with a dye log and a costing.

Your instructor watches you do it and marks against this week's three objectives, two marks each. The written check below is worth one mark: this is a practical subject and it is marked like one.

lessons.title: Materials, tools, and not getting hurt
lessons.summary: What each tool is for, how to hold it, and the rules that keep fingers attached.
objectives: You will name six tools and what each is for
You will cut away from your body with a controlled blade
You will set up and clear a safe work area
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Handle each tool: knife, scissors, rule, awl, pliers, needle
- Cut away from the body, on a board, with the free hand behind the blade
- Set up, then clear down completely

## Understand it

Every craft workshop has sharp, hot and heavy things in it. The rules that stop people getting hurt are simple, and they are the same everywhere.

**Cutting tools** (craft knife, scissors, blades):

![On a cutting mat, the free hand holds the steel rule behind the blade, and the blade travels away from it and away from the body.](media:arts/cutting-safety.svg)

- Cut **on a cutting board or mat**, never on your knee or hand.
- Cut **away from your body**, with the **free hand behind the blade**, never in front of it.
- Use a **sharp** blade — a blunt one needs force and slips. Snap off or replace blades and put old ones in a closed container.
- Retract or cap the blade the moment you put it down.

**Pointed tools** (awl, needles, pins): store points down or in a holder; count needles in and out.

**Pliers and wire:** wire ends spring — wear eye protection when cutting, and cover sharp ends.

**Glues, paints and solvents:** read the label; ventilate; keep off skin; no eating or drinking at the bench. Glue guns burn — use the stand, never touch the nozzle.

**Lifting and posture:** bend your knees to lift; take breaks from long bent-over work to protect your back and eyes.

**Setting up a safe bench:**

- Good **light**.
- **Clear space** — only the tools for this task out.
- Tools stored where they are always found.
- A **first-aid kit** within reach, and someone who knows where it is.

## Key words

- **Cutting mat:** a protective surface for cutting on
- **Free hand:** the hand not holding the tool, kept behind the blade
- **Ventilation:** fresh air to clear fumes
- **Awl:** a pointed tool for making holes

## Read and watch

- [Hazardous substances (COSHH)](https://www.hse.gov.uk/coshh/) — UK Health and Safety Executive
- [Manual handling at work](https://www.hse.gov.uk/msd/manual-handling/) — UK Health and Safety Executive
- [GCSE Design and Technology](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/subjects/zvg4d2p) — BBC Bitesize

## Practise at home

1. Set up and clear a work area at home three times
1. Practise controlled cutting on scrap card

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** Make a small version first. A mistake on a sample costs an hour; the same mistake on the real piece costs a week.
- **If you already can:** Make a second piece to a tighter tolerance, then write the instructions so somebody else could make it.

## Assessed this week

**Practical (6 marks) —** Set up a safe work area, make ten controlled cuts, and clear down fully.

Your instructor watches you do it and marks against this week's three objectives, two marks each. The written check below is worth one mark: this is a practical subject and it is marked like one.

lessons.title: Measuring, marking and cutting straight
lessons.summary: The skill everything else rests on: accuracy.
objectives: You will measure and mark to the millimetre
You will cut a straight line against a rule
You will check your own work against the measurement
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Mark with a sharp pencil, not a thick one — a thick line is a millimetre of error
- Cut against a metal rule, several light passes, not one heavy one
- Measure your finished cut and write down the error

## Understand it

"Measure twice, cut once." Most errors in making start before the cut — in the **marking**.

**Measuring accurately:**

- Use a **steel rule** or tape; plastic rules wear and bend.
- Measure from a **true edge** or the zero end of the rule — check that the end of a tape is not worn.
- Read the scale **straight on**, with your eye directly above the mark — reading from an angle (parallax) shifts the reading.
- Work in **millimetres** — easier than mixed centimetres and fractions.

**Marking:**

![Reading a rule from directly above gives the true measurement; from an angle (parallax) it shifts. Mark the waste side of a line with a cross and cut on that side.](media:arts/measure-mark.svg)

- A **sharp, hard pencil** (or a scribe on metal) — a thick line can be a whole millimetre wide, and which side do you cut?
- Mark with a small **V** or tick to show exactly where.
- Use a **set square** for right angles — measure from one squared edge, not from a ragged one.
- Mark the **waste side** with a cross so you cut on the right side of the line.

**Cutting straight:**

- Cut against a **metal rule**, held firmly with fingers away from the edge.
- Make **several light passes**, not one heavy cut — a heavy cut wanders and slips; light passes follow the rule and give a clean edge.
- Keep the blade **vertical**.

The test: measure your finished piece. Within 1 mm of the plan is good work; within 0.5 mm is excellent.

## Key words

- **Steel rule:** a metal ruler that stays straight and accurate
- **Set square:** a tool for marking right angles
- **Parallax:** a reading error from looking at a scale at an angle
- **Waste side:** the side of the line that will be cut away

## Read and watch

- [GCSE Design and Technology](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/subjects/zvg4d2p) — BBC Bitesize

## Practise at home

1. Cut five 100mm squares and measure each one
1. Write down how far off each was

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** Make a small version first. A mistake on a sample costs an hour; the same mistake on the real piece costs a week.
- **If you already can:** Make a second piece to a tighter tolerance, then write the instructions so somebody else could make it.

## Assessed this week

Your instructor watches you do it and marks against this week's three objectives, two marks each. The written check below is worth one mark: this is a practical subject and it is marked like one.

lessons.title: Beadwork
lessons.summary: Threading, tension and pattern — and why even tension is the whole craft.
objectives: You will thread and finish a bead piece securely
You will hold even tension throughout
You will follow a repeating pattern
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Thread a simple pattern, keeping tension the same bead to bead
- Finish the ends so they will not come undone
- Follow a repeat of at least four beads

## Understand it

Beads have been made and worn in Africa for tens of thousands of years — shell beads found in caves in North and South Africa are among the oldest known human ornaments. In Nigeria, **coral and glass beads** are central to Yoruba, Edo and other cultures: the beaded crowns of Yoruba kings, the coral regalia of the Oba of Benin, and the beaded jewellery worn at weddings and festivals.

**Basic beadwork:**

- **Materials** — beads (glass, seed beads, wood, plastic, recycled paper), strong thread or beading wire, a beading needle, clasps, crimp beads.
- **Tension** — the key skill. Thread pulled too tight makes a stiff piece that kinks; too loose and beads gap and wobble. Keep the **same tension bead to bead**.
- **Pattern repeat** — plan a sequence (e.g. red–red–gold–black) and repeat it exactly. Lay it out on a cloth or bead board before threading.
- **Finishing** — the most important part. Pass the thread back through several beads and tie secure knots between them; use **crimp beads** on wire. A piece that comes undone is worthless.

![A planned repeat (red, red, gold, black) laid out before threading, and three tensions: too tight kinks and stiffens, even lies flat and straight, too loose leaves gaps.](media:arts/bead-tension.svg)

**Techniques to try:** simple stringing; **peyote stitch** and **brick stitch** (beads woven into flat fabric); **loom beading**.

Respect meaning: some beads and colours carry status or ritual meaning — certain coral regalia, for instance, belongs to royalty and chiefs. Learn what you are copying.

## Key words

- **Tension:** how tightly the thread holds the beads
- **Repeat:** a sequence of beads repeated exactly
- **Crimp bead:** a soft metal bead squeezed to secure wire
- **Peyote stitch:** a technique weaving beads into a flat fabric

## Read and watch

- [Search the collections: Yoruba beadwork](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/search/?q=yoruba%20beadwork) — Victoria and Albert Museum

- [Art of Africa](https://www.khanacademy.org/humanities/art-africa) — Khan Academy

## Practise at home

1. Make one bracelet at home and check the tension is even
1. Try the same pattern twice and compare

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** Make a small version first. A mistake on a sample costs an hour; the same mistake on the real piece costs a week.
- **If you already can:** Make a second piece to a tighter tolerance, then write the instructions so somebody else could make it.

Your instructor watches you do it and marks against this week's three objectives, two marks each. The written check below is worth one mark: this is a practical subject and it is marked like one.

lessons.title: Weaving
lessons.summary: Warp, weft, and making a stable woven square from raffia or yarn.
objectives: You will set up a warp with even spacing
You will weave a plain weave
You will keep the edges straight
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Set up a card loom with evenly spaced warp threads
- Weave over-under, beating down each row
- Do not pull the weft tight — that pulls the edges in

## Understand it

All weaving is two sets of threads crossing at right angles:

- The **warp** — threads held under tension on the loom, running lengthways.
- The **weft** — the thread passed across, over and under the warp threads.

The simplest pattern is **plain (tabby) weave**: over one, under one; next row under one, over one.

Nigeria has great weaving traditions: Yoruba **aso oke** (woven in narrow strips on men's horizontal looms, then sewn together — worn at weddings and ceremonies), Igbo **akwete** cloth (woven on wide upright looms by women), and Ebira and Hausa weaving.

**Weaving on a card loom:**

1. Cut notches evenly along two opposite edges of stiff card. Wind the warp round them — **even spacing and even tension** matter most.
2. Weave the weft over-under with a needle or flat stick.
3. **Beat down** each row with a fork or comb so rows sit close and even.
4. Leave the weft in a gentle **arc** ("bubbling") before beating — do **not pull it tight**, or the edges draw in and the piece becomes waisted, narrower in the middle.
5. Watch the edges (**selvedges**) — they should stay straight.

**Patterns:** stripes (change weft colour), checks (change both warp and weft colours), and **twill** (over two, under two, shifting one each row) which makes diagonal lines.

![Two woven squares: plain weave alternates over one, under one, row by row; twill goes over two, under two, shifting one thread each row, which makes diagonal lines.](media:arts/warp-weft.svg)

## Key words

- **Warp:** the threads held lengthways on the loom
- **Weft:** the thread woven across the warp
- **Selvedge:** the finished side edge of woven cloth
- **Aso oke:** Yoruba strip-woven ceremonial cloth

## Read and watch

- [Search: aso oke](https://artsandculture.google.com/search?q=aso%20oke) — Google Arts & Culture
- [Search the collections: weaving](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/search/?q=weaving) — Victoria and Albert Museum
- [Textiles collection](https://www.vam.ac.uk/collections/textiles) — Victoria and Albert Museum

## Practise at home

1. Weave one 10cm square at home
1. Measure the width at the top, middle and bottom

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** Make a small version first. A mistake on a sample costs an hour; the same mistake on the real piece costs a week.
- **If you already can:** Make a second piece to a tighter tolerance, then write the instructions so somebody else could make it.

lessons.title: Paper and card: simple bookbinding
lessons.summary: Folding, scoring and stitching a notebook that opens flat and stays together.
objectives: You will score and fold accurately
You will stitch a pamphlet binding
You will trim a clean edge
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Score before folding — a scored fold is sharp, an unscored one is ragged
- Stitch a three-hole pamphlet binding
- Trim the fore edge square

## Understand it

A notebook you make yourself is useful, sellable and teaches precision.

**Paper has a grain** — the direction its fibres mostly run. It folds and bends more easily **along** the grain. Test: bend a sheet gently both ways; the easier way is with the grain. For books, the grain should run **parallel to the spine**, so pages turn and lie flat.

**Scoring before folding:** run a **bone folder** (or the back of a blunt knife) along a metal rule to press a line into the card. The fold then follows the line exactly and is crisp. Folding card without scoring cracks the surface and gives a ragged edge.

**Three-hole pamphlet stitch** — the simplest binding:

![The pamphlet stitch on three holes along the fold: in through the centre, out through one end hole, back in through the other end hole along the long stitch, out through the centre, and tie across the long stitch.](media:arts/pamphlet-stitch.svg)

1. Fold several sheets (a **signature**) together with a cover, score and crease.
2. Mark three holes on the fold: centre and two equally spaced; pierce them with an **awl** (on a board or in an open phone book, never into your hand).
3. Sew with waxed thread: **in through the centre, out through one end, in through the other end hole, out through the centre**.
4. Tie the ends **across the long stitch** at the centre, trim.

**Trimming the fore edge** — the pages in the middle stick out further ("creep"). Trim the front edge straight with a steel rule and sharp knife in several light passes.

Larger books join many signatures with longer stitching — the same principle, scaled up.

## Key words

- **Grain:** the direction paper's fibres run
- **Score:** pressing a line so card folds crisply
- **Signature:** a group of folded sheets sewn together
- **Fore edge:** the front edge of a book opposite the spine

## Read and watch

- [Collections care](https://www.loc.gov/preservation/care/) — Library of Congress
- [GCSE Design and Technology](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/subjects/zvg4d2p) — BBC Bitesize

## Practise at home

1. Make one notebook at home
1. Compare a scored fold with an unscored one

## Make it fit you

- **If you already can:** Make a second piece to a tighter tolerance, then write the instructions so somebody else could make it.

lessons.title: Making from what is thrown away
lessons.summary: Tyres, bottles, sachets and offcuts — design that starts from the material you can actually get.
objectives: You will design around a found material

You will say why the material should lead the design
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Collect and clean one waste material properly
- Design something the material is actually good at
- Build a prototype

## Understand it

Waste is a raw material that nobody has priced yet. Nigerian makers turn plastic bottles, sachet water bags, tyres, cans, fabric offcuts and newspaper into furniture, bags, jewellery, art and building materials.

**Good upcycling starts with the material's strengths:**

- **Pure water sachets and plastic bags** — waterproof, flexible; can be fused (with care and ventilation) or woven into mats and bags.
- **Plastic bottles** — rigid, clear, waterproof; containers, planters, building bricks when packed with sand.
- **Tyres and inner tubes** — tough, flexible, waterproof; seats, planters, sandals, bags.
- **Fabric offcuts** (from tailors) — patchwork, rugs, stuffing, ropes.
- **Paper and card** — papier-mâché, rolled beads, recycled paper.
- **Cans and metal** — cut edges are very sharp; wear gloves and file edges smooth.

**Process:**

![Upcycling in four steps: collect and clean the waste properly, test what it can do, design something that uses its strengths, then prototype and improve.](media:arts/upcycle-process.svg)

1. **Collect and clean** properly — wash, dry, remove labels and residues. Dirty waste makes dirty products.
2. **Test** the material: does it bend, cut, glue, stitch, melt?
3. **Design** something the material is good at — not forcing it to be something it is not.
4. **Prototype**, test, improve.

**Safety:** never burn plastic to shape it — the fumes are toxic. Avoid containers that held chemicals.

Why it matters: waste that becomes a product is waste that did not end up in a drain or on a burning heap.

## Key words

- **Upcycling:** turning waste into something of greater value
- **Prototype:** a first working version, to test and improve
- **Material property:** how a material behaves — rigid, flexible, waterproof

## Read and watch

- [GCSE Design and Technology](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/subjects/zvg4d2p) — BBC Bitesize

lessons.title: Remaking week 3, to a finish
lessons.summary: Returning to the beadwork with the accuracy and tension you have since built.
objectives: You will remake the week 3 piece to a higher finish
You will compare the two side by side
You will name the three things you now do differently
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Remake the week 3 bead piece
- Lay the two side by side and be honest about the difference
- Write down three specific changes in your method

## Understand it

In week 3 you made a bead piece. Since then you have measured, cut, woven and bound to tighter standards. Remaking the same piece now shows how much your hand and eye have changed — and finishing it fully, to a standard someone would pay for, is a skill in itself.

**Remake it with intention:**

- Plan the **repeat** on paper first, and count the beads.
- Keep **tension** even — check every few centimetres by laying it flat: does it lie straight, without kinks or gaps?
- **Finish** properly: secure knots hidden inside beads, clean clasps, no visible glue, no loose ends.

**Compare honestly.** Lay the two pieces side by side and look as a buyer would:

- Is the pattern regular?
- Does it hang well?
- Are the ends secure and neat?
- Would you pay for it? How much?

**Write three specific changes in your method** — not "I was more careful" but "I laid out the sequence before threading", "I used a crimp bead instead of a knot", "I checked tension every 10 beads". Specific notes are what turn practice into progress.

Craftspeople call this the difference between **making** and **finishing**. Most beginners can make; few finish well. Finishing is where the value is.

## Key words

- **Revisit:** remaking earlier work with improved skill

lessons.title: Joining things so they stay joined
lessons.summary: Glue, stitch, wire and knot — choosing the right one and doing it properly.
objectives: You will choose a joining method for a given material
You will make a joint that survives handling
You will say why the wrong glue fails
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Match the method to the material: glue, stitch, wire, knot
- Make three joints and test each to destruction
- Learn which glue works on which surface

## Understand it

Most made things fail at their **joints**. Choosing the right joining method for the material is a core skill.

**Methods:**

- **Glue (adhesive)** — different glues for different materials:
  - **PVA (white glue)** — paper, card, wood, fabric. Slow to dry; needs clamping.
  - **Contact adhesive** — leather, rubber, laminates. Apply to both surfaces, let it go tacky, press together. Strong fumes — ventilate.
  - **Epoxy (two-part)** — metal, glass, ceramics, hard plastics. Very strong; mix exactly.
  - **Hot glue** — quick and convenient, but weak and brittle under heat or stress.
  - **Superglue** — tiny, quick bonds on hard, close-fitting surfaces; bonds skin instantly.
- **Stitching** — fabric, leather, paper; flexible and strong.
- **Wire and twisting** — beads, metal, baskets.
- **Knots** — cord, rope, weaving, macramé.
- **Mechanical** — screws, rivets, nails, slotted joints: can be undone and repaired.

**Gluing well:**

![PVA for paper, card and wood; contact adhesive for leather and rubber; epoxy for metal and glass; stitching for fabric and leather; screws or rivets where it must come apart.](media:arts/joint-chooser.svg)

- Surfaces **clean, dry and slightly rough** (sanded) so glue grips.
- **Thin, even** layer — thick glue is weaker, not stronger.
- **Clamp or hold** while it sets; follow the setting time.

**Test to destruction** — pull, bend and twist sample joints until they break. Where it fails tells you: glue that peels cleanly needs better surface preparation; material tearing beside the joint means the joint was stronger than the material.

## Key words

- **Adhesive:** a glue or bonding substance
- **PVA:** white glue for paper, card, wood and fabric
- **Epoxy:** a strong two-part glue for hard materials
- **Test to destruction:** stressing a sample until it breaks to learn its limit

lessons.title: Finish and surface
lessons.summary: Sanding, sealing and edges — the difference between a school project and a product.
objectives: You will finish an edge so it is smooth and even
You will apply a sealant or finish evenly
You will say what a buyer notices first
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Sand through the grades, not straight to fine
- Apply a thin even finish, then a second thin coat — never one thick one
- Check the edges; that is what a buyer runs a thumb along

## Understand it

A surface finish protects a piece and makes it beautiful — and a poor finish ruins good making.

**Sanding through the grades:**

![Sandpaper grades 80 → 120 → 180 → 240: each finer grade removes the scratches left by the one before, which is why skipping a grade leaves scratches the finish shows up.](media:arts/grit-steps.svg)

- Sandpaper is graded by **grit number** — low numbers (60–80) are coarse, high (240–400+) are fine.
- Start coarse enough to remove marks, then move **step by step** through the grades (e.g. 80 → 120 → 180 → 240). Each grade removes the scratches of the one before.
- Jumping from coarse to fine leaves deep scratches the fine paper cannot remove — they show up clearly once finish is applied.
- On wood, sand **with the grain**.
- Remove dust between grades and before finishing.

**Applying finish** (paint, varnish, oil, wax):

- **Thin coats.** Two or three thin coats beat one thick one. Thick coats run, drip, stay sticky, wrinkle and take far longer to dry.
- Let each coat **dry fully**, lightly sand with very fine paper, dust off, then apply the next.
- Work in a **dust-free, ventilated** space; many finishes give off fumes.
- Brush in long strokes in one direction; do not keep re-brushing as it starts to dry.

**Check the edges.** Edges, corners and the underside are where buyers look to judge quality — and where makers rush. Run your fingers along them: they should be smooth and evenly finished.

## Key words

- **Grit:** the coarseness of sandpaper — lower is coarser
- **Coat:** one layer of paint or finish
- **Run:** a drip in a finish from applying too thickly

lessons.title: Designing for somebody else
lessons.summary: Making what a buyer wants rather than what you feel like making.
objectives: You will interview one person about what they would buy
You will change a design based on what they said
You will say why your own taste is not the brief
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Interview two people: what would you buy, and for how much?
- Change one design based on their answers
- Keep a note of what you changed and why

. **With an AI assistant —** ask it for ten things your waste material could become, keep the two worth making, and test those on a real buyer. The ideas are cheap; the buyer is the evidence.

## Understand it

Making for yourself, you decide what is good. Making for **someone else**, *they* decide — and they decide with their money. Designers call learning what users need **user research**, and it begins with a conversation.

**Interviewing potential buyers:**

- Ask **open questions**: "What would you use this for?", "What do you not like about the ones you have?", "Where would you buy something like this?"
- Ask about **price**: "What would you expect to pay?" — and watch their face as well as their words.
- Ask about **real past behaviour**, not wishes: "When did you last buy a bag? What made you choose it?" People are poor at predicting what they will buy, and good at describing what they did.
- **Do not sell** while you research. If you defend your design, people stop being honest.
- **Listen more than you talk**; write down their words.

**Acting on what you hear:**

- Look for what **more than one person** says.
- Change **one** thing in your design at a time, so you know what made the difference.
- Keep a **design log**: what you changed, why, and what people said about the new version.

This is how the design process works in industry: research, design, prototype, test, improve — a loop, not a straight line.

![The design loop: research with real buyers, design, prototype, test, improve — changing one thing at a time and logging what changed — then round again.](media:arts/design-loop.svg)

## Key words

- **User research:** learning what the people you design for need
- **Open question:** a question that cannot be answered yes or no
- **Iteration:** improving a design through repeated cycles
- **Design log:** a record of changes and the reasons for them

lessons.title: Pricing and packaging
lessons.summary: Costing honestly and presenting the piece so it looks worth the money.
objectives: You will cost a piece including your time
You will set a price with a margin
You will package it presentably
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Add up materials, then add your hours at a real rate
- Set a price that covers cost plus a margin
- Package it — a good piece in a plastic bag sells for less

## Understand it

Hand-made goods are often priced at the cost of materials — which means the maker works for free. A price must cover **everything**.

**The pricing formula:**

![An example bag: materials ₦2,500, labour 4 hours × ₦1,000 = ₦4,000, overheads ₦500 make a cost of ₦7,000; a 40% margin of ₦2,800 gives a price of ₦9,800.](media:arts/craft-pricing.svg)

1. **Materials** — every bead, thread, glue, paint, packaging item. Divide bulk purchases by how many pieces they make.
2. **Labour** — your hours × a **real hourly rate**. Time yourself making a few pieces. If a bag takes 4 hours, and you value your time at ₦1,000 an hour, labour is ₦4,000.
3. **Overheads** — tools, transport, market fees, electricity, a share of things that wear out.
4. **Cost** = materials + labour + overheads.
5. **Price** = cost + **margin** (profit, often 20–50% or more), which pays for growth and slow weeks.

Selling to a **shop** (wholesale) usually means they pay you around half the shop price, so your wholesale price must still cover your cost.

**Check the market** — what do similar pieces sell for? If your cost is above the market price, make more efficiently, use different materials, or sell to a different market (quality, story, custom orders) — do not just cut the price below cost.

**Packaging** is part of the product:

- It **protects** (tissue, a box, a cloth bag).
- It **tells the story** — a card with your name, the materials, how it was made, care instructions.
- It makes a **gift** — and gifts are a large share of craft sales.

## Key words

- **Labour cost:** your hours multiplied by your hourly rate
- **Overheads:** running costs beyond materials
- **Margin:** the profit added on top of cost
- **Wholesale:** selling to a shop that resells

lessons.title: The craft market
lessons.summary: Selling your work to real people and finding out what the market says.
objectives: You will present a finished piece for sale
You will explain how it was made and priced
You will record what people actually said
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Set up a stall with your finished pieces, priced and packaged
- Explain your making and pricing to anyone who asks
- Write down every piece of feedback, especially the unwelcome kind

## Understand it

A market stall is a small shop, and running it teaches more about your products than any amount of planning.

**Setting up:**

![A market stall from the front: the best pieces at eye level on stands and boxes, everything else grouped on the table, and a price tag on every piece.](media:arts/market-stall.svg)

- **Display at eye level** where possible; use height (boxes, stands, a rail) rather than laying everything flat.
- **Group** pieces — by colour, type or price.
- Show items **in use** — a bag with things in it, jewellery on a stand or a person.
- **Prices clearly visible** on every piece. Many shoppers will not ask and simply walk away.
- A clean cloth, a sign with your name, and a way to take payment (cash with change, and a transfer account or POS).

**Talking to customers:**

- Greet people; let them look without pressure.
- Tell the **story** — the materials, how you made it, what the pattern means.
- Explain **why** it costs what it does, briefly and confidently.

**Record everything** — this is free market research:

- What **sold**, at what price, and what did not.
- What people **picked up** but put down — and why, if they said.
- Questions people asked; requests for colours, sizes or items you did not have.
- **Comments** — good and bad, word for word.

Afterwards, review: what will you make more of? What will you stop making? What will you change? The answers come from customers, not from guessing.

## Key words

- **Display:** how products are arranged to attract buyers
- **Market research:** learning what customers want
- **Sales record:** a log of what sold, when and for how much
